passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of the novel antioxidant compound, X-100, on the viability of cultured human fibroblasts over a 24‑hour period. The study employed a dose‑response design with five treatment groups: 0 µM (vehicle control), 10 µM, 30 µM, 60 µM, and 100 µM. Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay, and absorbance values were recorded at 570 nm. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate a biphasic (U-shaped) response: viability decreases at low concentrations but increases at higher concentrations. The researchers identified the lowest viability (at 30 µM) and the maximal viability achieved at 100 µM. They also performed a statistical analysis (ANOVA) to determine significance between groups. Table 1 gives the mean viability of each group (n = 6 per group).

qs.q: Based on Table 1, what is the approximate viability percentage of fibroblasts after 24 hours of exposure to 60 µM X-100?
qs.x: The table shows that at 60 µM, the viability is 95% after 24 hours. This is the correct reading of the data. Trap: Option B (85%) corresponds to the 10 µM concentration and is a common misreading of the table.

qs.q: Which design feature of the study allows the researchers to detect that viability first falls and then rises with concentration, rather than following a single straight-line trend?
o: Inclusion of a vehicle control (0 µM) group
Measuring viability at a single time point of 24 hours
Testing five concentrations, several between 10 and 100 µM
Use of the MTT assay with absorbance read at 570 nm
qs.x: Correct: Seeing a fall followed by a rise requires measurements at several intermediate concentrations; with only two or three doses the shape of the curve could not be resolved. Table 1 shows 100, 85, 70, 95 and 110%. Why the others are wrong: A) a vehicle control supplies one baseline point and says nothing about the shape of the curve. B) a single time point fixes duration, not the number of doses sampled. D) the MTT readout measures viability but does not determine how many doses are compared. Trap: Choosing the vehicle control because controls are always 'important', although it supplies only one baseline point and not the shape of the dose-response curve.

qs.q: Calculate the percent change in viability from the 10 µM to the 60 µM concentration group.
qs.x: Percent change = (95 − 85)/85 × 100 = 11.8%, which rounds to 12%. Trap: Reporting the 10-point absolute rise as a 10% increase, or dividing by the 60 µM value (95) instead of the starting 10 µM value (85), rather than computing 10/85 ≈ 12%.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: Higher concentrations of X-100 always increase viability.
The lowest viability occurred at 30 µM.
The study used six replicates per group.
ANOVA was used to assess statistical significance.
qs.x: Correct: Viability fell from 100% to 85% and 70% at 10 and 30 µM before rising to 95% and 110%, so higher concentrations do not always increase viability. Why the others are wrong: B) Table 1 shows 70% at 30 µM, the lowest value, so this is supported. C) the passage states n = 6 per group. D) the passage states that ANOVA was used. Trap: Assuming a dose-response relationship must be monotonic and reading the rise at 60 and 100 µM as applying to every higher concentration.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which statement about viability after 24 hours is correct?
o: Viability at 100 µM was higher than in the 0 µM vehicle control.
Viability at 30 µM was higher than at 10 µM.
Viability at 60 µM was lower than at 30 µM.
Viability fell steadily as concentration rose from 0 to 100 µM.
qs.x: Correct: Viability at 100 µM was 110%, above the 100% vehicle control. Why the others are wrong: B) viability was 70% at 30 µM, lower than 85% at 10 µM. C) viability was 95% at 60 µM, higher than 70% at 30 µM. D) viability fell only to 30 µM and then rose, so it did not fall steadily. Trap: Assuming a compound that reduces viability at low dose must keep reducing it, ignoring the rise at 60 and 100 µM.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Greenfield investigated the effect of light intensity on the photosynthetic rate of *Arabidopsis thaliana*. The experiment was conducted in a controlled growth chamber where plants were exposed to four different light intensities: 100, 200, 400, and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. After a 48‑hour acclimation period, the net CO₂ assimilation rate was measured using a portable infrared gas analyzer. The data were summarized in Table 1 below. The researchers noted a nonlinear increase in photosynthetic rate with light intensity, suggesting the presence of a light saturation point. They also observed that the standard deviation increased at the highest light intensity, indicating greater variability among individual plants. The authors concluded that optimizing light intensity could enhance crop yield, but further studies are needed to determine the optimal intensity for different cultivars.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which of the following best describes the relationship between light intensity and photosynthetic rate?
o: Photosynthetic rate increases linearly with light intensity.
Rate rises steeply at low intensity, then gains diminish as intensity increases.
Photosynthetic rate decreases at high intensities due to photoinhibition.
Photosynthetic rate is independent of light intensity.
qs.x: Correct: B) The rate rises 2.6 units from 100 to 200, 3.3 from 200 to 400, but only 1.4 from 400 to 800 even though intensity doubles, so gains diminish as the curve approaches saturation. Why the others are wrong: A) Equal increments per light increment are not seen; the slope falls. C) The rate at 800 (10.5) is higher than at 400 (9.1), so there is no decrease. D) The rate changes more than threefold across the range. Trap: Assuming a linear relationship (Option A) ignores the diminishing gains at higher intensities; calling the curve fully flat (a plateau) overlooks that the rate still rose from 9.1 to 10.5.

qs.q: If the researchers wanted to determine whether light intensity has a statistically significant effect on photosynthetic rate, which experimental design element should they include?
o: Randomly assign plants to each light intensity group.
Use only a single plant per intensity to reduce variability.
Measure photosynthetic rate at only the highest light intensity.
Exclude the 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ group to simplify analysis.
qs.x: Random assignment controls for confounding variables and ensures that differences in photosynthetic rate are attributable to light intensity rather than plant-to-plant variation. Trap: Using a single plant per group (Option B) would increase sampling error and reduce statistical power.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in average photosynthetic rate from 100 to 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
qs.x: Correct: A) Percent increase = (5.8 - 3.2) / 3.2 x 100 = 81.25%, about 81.3%. Why the others are wrong: B) 125.0% does not follow from the table values. C) 44.8% divides the 2.6 change by the final value (5.8) instead of the baseline. D) 68.8% does not follow from the table values. Trap: Dividing the change by the final value (2.6 / 5.8 = 44.8%, option C) instead of the baseline understates the increase.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is a common misconception about the data presented?
o: The standard deviation at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ indicates higher variability among plants.
The increase from 400 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is smaller than from 100 to 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
The photosynthetic rate at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is the highest among all groups.
The data suggest a linear relationship between light intensity and photosynthetic rate.
qs.x: The data clearly show a nonlinear, saturating relationship, not a linear one. Option D is the misconception. Trap: Option B might mislead students into thinking the rate decreases, but it actually increases, just at a slower rate.

qs.q: At 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ the net CO₂ assimilation rate rises only from 9.1 to 10.5 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ even though light doubles. Which factor most likely limits photosynthesis at this point?
o: The rate of photon absorption by chlorophyll, which is still proportional to light intensity
The capacity of the Calvin cycle (Rubisco activity and CO₂ supply) to use the ATP and NADPH being generated
The amount of O₂ available to the light-dependent reactions
The number of water molecules in the thylakoid lumen
qs.x: At saturating light the light-dependent reactions supply ATP and NADPH faster than the Calvin cycle can consume them, so carbon fixation (Rubisco activity, CO₂ supply, RuBP regeneration) becomes limiting and the light-response curve plateaus. Trap: Option A treats light absorption as limiting, but that is true only on the linear, light-limited part of the curve.

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Color vision depends on three cone types with peak sensitivities near 420 nm (S), 530 nm (M) and 560 nm (L). Color is coded by comparing their outputs (trichromatic theory), and opponent processing in the retina and thalamus compares red with green and blue with yellow. Red-green color blindness usually results from missing or altered L or M pigments encoded on the X chromosome.
Researchers tested color matching in four participants (Table 1).

qs.q: Why can participant B not distinguish red from green?
o: The M and L comparison is missing
Red light does not reach the retina
Rods cannot detect color at all
Rods are irrelevant to this comparison.
qs.x: Correct: Red-green discrimination depends on comparing signals from the M and L cones; with only one of them, the comparison cannot be made. Why the others are wrong: S cones are present; rods do not mediate color; light reaches the retina. Trap: Assuming a specific cone detects a specific color by itself.

qs.q: Why can participants B and C still tell blue from yellow?
o: Yellow light stimulates only S cones
Yellow stimulates M and L cones more.
Blue and yellow are detected by rods
The S cone output can be compared
They have all three cone types
qs.x: Correct: The blue-yellow channel compares S cone output with the combined output of the remaining longer-wavelength cone, which is intact in both. Why the others are wrong: Each lacks a cone type; rods do not encode color; yellow stimulates longer-wavelength cones. Trap: Expecting the loss of one channel to remove all color vision.

qs.q: How does trichromatic theory explain color perception?
o: A single receptor cannot distinguish color.
The lens separates light into colors
Colors are detected by rods at low light
qs.x: Correct: Any wavelength produces a characteristic pattern of activity across the three cone types, and the brain reads the ratios as color. Why the others are wrong: A single receptor type cannot separate wavelength from intensity; rods are monochromatic; the lens focuses. Trap: Thinking each cone signals one specific color.

qs.q: Why is red-green color blindness more common in men?
o: Lenses do not differ this way.
Correct: men have one X chromosome.
The condition is caused by testosterone
qs.x: Correct: The M and L pigment genes lie on the X chromosome, so a single variant allele affects men, while women usually have a normal copy on the second X. Why the others are wrong: Cone counts, lens filtering and hormones are not the cause. Trap: Looking for a physiological rather than a genetic explanation.

qs.q: What does participant D's result suggest?
o: Light and form are still detected.
S cones alone detect blue and yellow
One cone type gives full color vision
Correct: comparison is impossible with one.
qs.x: Correct: With only one cone type, every wavelength produces a signal that differs only in magnitude, which cannot be separated from a change in brightness. Why the others are wrong: One type is insufficient; vision for form remains; both color channels failed. Trap: Confusing loss of color vision with blindness.

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity from decision bias. On each trial a signal may or may not be present, and the observer reports yes or no, giving hits, misses, false alarms and correct rejections. Sensitivity (d′) rises with the difference between signal and noise distributions; a liberal criterion raises both hits and false alarms, while a conservative one lowers both.
Observers detected a faint tone in noise under two instruction sets (Table 1). Each had 100 signal trials and 100 noise-only trials.

qs.q: Why does observer 1's hit rate fall under the stricter instruction?
o: The tone was quieter in the second session
The noise was removed in the second session
qs.x: Correct: Requiring certainty shifts the criterion so fewer trials are reported as signals; both hits and false alarms fall while d′ stays near the same value. Why the others are wrong: d′ was similar; tone and noise were unchanged. Trap: Reading a lower hit rate as worse hearing.

qs.q: What does the similar d′ across instructions show?
qs.x: Correct: The point of signal detection theory is that d′ estimates the observer's sensory discriminability while the criterion captures willingness to say yes; here only the latter changed. Why the others are wrong: Sensitivity was stable; neither hits nor false alarms alone measure sensitivity. Trap: Using the hit rate as a measure of sensitivity.

qs.q: Which outcome is a false alarm?
o: Reporting no tone when one was present
Reporting a tone when one was present
Reporting no tone when none was present
Reporting a tone when none was present
Correct: a yes on a noise trial.
qs.x: Correct: A false alarm is a yes response on a trial with no signal. Why the others are wrong: Each names a different outcome category. Trap: Mixing up misses and false alarms.

qs.q: A radiologist is told that missing a tumor is far worse than a false alarm. How should the criterion shift?
o: Toward liberal, accepting more false alarms
Toward conservative, to reduce false alarms
No shift, since d′ is fixed
qs.x: Correct: When misses are costlier than false alarms, lowering the threshold for saying yes raises the hit rate at the cost of more false alarms. Why the others are wrong: A conservative shift increases misses; the criterion is adjustable; it does not change d′. Trap: Treating fewer false alarms as always better.

qs.q: Why does observer 2 have a lower d′ than observer 1?
o: Criterion affects hits and false alarms, not d′.
More signal trials in that session
qs.x: Correct: Under the same instruction, observer 2 had both fewer hits and fewer false alarms than expected for equal sensitivity, giving a smaller d′. Why the others are wrong: Criterion does not change d′; trials and intensity were constant. Trap: Confusing criterion differences with sensitivity differences.

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania or hypomania alternating with depression. Lithium reduces the frequency of episodes and lowers suicide risk, but it has a narrow therapeutic index: serum levels must be monitored because toxicity occurs not far above the therapeutic range. Dehydration, NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics raise lithium levels.
In a 1-year randomized trial, 300 patients received lithium, valproate or placebo (Table 1).

qs.q: Why must serum lithium be monitored?
o: Lithium levels do not change over time
They change with hydration and drugs.
Lithium is not absorbed reliably at all
Therapeutic and toxic levels are close
qs.x: Correct: Because levels only modestly above about 1.2 mmol/L can cause toxicity, regular measurement is needed to keep the dose in range. Why the others are wrong: Absorption is reliable; monitoring prevents harm rather than adding efficacy; levels vary. Trap: Thinking monitoring improves the drug's action.

qs.q: Why would a thiazide diuretic raise lithium levels?
o: Thiazides convert lithium into a toxin
Correct: the kidney handles them similarly.
Thiazides block lithium absorption from the gut
qs.x: Correct: Lithium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule along pathways shared with sodium, so sodium depletion increases lithium retention and raises serum levels. Why the others are wrong: Thiazides act renally and reduce excretion; no conversion occurs. Trap: Reversing the direction of the interaction.

qs.q: Which result shows lithium's benefit most directly?
qs.x: Correct: Halving the proportion of patients with any mood episode relative to placebo is the primary efficacy finding. Why the others are wrong: Serum level and discontinuation rates address dosing and tolerability; the placebo contrast is the key one. Trap: Choosing a safety measure as the efficacy result.

qs.q: Why is a higher discontinuation rate on active drugs expected?
o: Placebo is more toxic than lithium
qs.x: Correct: Pharmacologically active treatments produce adverse effects such as tremor, weight gain and thirst, so more patients stop them than stop an inert pill. Why the others are wrong: Placebo is inert; discontinuation reflects tolerability; allocation was random. Trap: Interpreting discontinuation as treatment failure.

qs.q: Why is randomization important in this trial?
o: It replaces the need for a placebo
A placebo arm was still used.
qs.x: Correct: Patients differ in episode history and severity, which strongly predicts outcome, so random allocation makes the comparison fair. Why the others are wrong: Not all improved; the placebo arm remained; side effects occurred. Trap: Confusing randomization with blinding or with guaranteeing benefit.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers conducted a study to evaluate the efficacy of a novel cognitive-behavioral intervention (CBI) on reducing anxiety symptoms among adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Eighty participants were enrolled from two clinics: patients at one clinic formed the CBI group (n=40), and patients at the other formed a wait‑list control group (n=40). Baseline assessments revealed comparable anxiety scores across groups (CBI mean 50.2, SD 5.1; control mean 50.4, SD 5.3). Over a 12‑week intervention period, participants in the CBI group received weekly 60‑minute sessions delivered by trained therapists, while controls received no intervention. Post‑intervention anxiety scores were significantly lower in the CBI group (mean 40.5, SD 4.8) compared to controls (mean 52.0, SD 5.3), yielding a p‑value <0.001. A clinically significant response was defined as a drop of at least 5 points from baseline; 30 of 40 CBI participants and 6 of 40 controls met this criterion. The study also measured secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms and functional impairment, which showed similar patterns of improvement. The authors noted limitations such as a relatively short follow‑up period and the absence of blinding. Despite these constraints, the findings suggest that CBI may be an effective treatment for GAD, warranting further research with larger samples and longer follow‑up.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the effect of the CBI on anxiety scores as shown in Table 1?
qs.x: Correct: B) The CBI group's mean fell from 50.2 to 40.5, and at 12 weeks it was well below the control mean (52.0); the between-group p < 0.001 shows this difference is statistically significant. Why the others are wrong: A) scores fell, not rose. C) the CBI mean dropped by about 10 points. D) baseline, post-treatment and p-values are all reported. Trap: Reading the lower post-treatment number as worse anxiety, when on this scale a lower score means fewer symptoms.

qs.q: Which design best matches the study described in the passage?
o: Patients were not selected by outcome.
Patients were not assigned by chance.
Correct: an intervention was given, but each clinic formed one group.
qs.x: Correct: The CBI was delivered by the study, but groups were patients at two different clinics. Similar baseline scores help, yet clinics could differ in other ways, so this is quasi-experimental. Why the others are wrong: No random assignment; selection by clinic, not outcome; and the exposure was assigned by the study rather than observed. Trap: Assuming comparable baseline means prove randomization.

qs.q: Calculate the relative risk (RR) of achieving a clinically significant reduction in anxiety for participants in the CBI group compared to the control group. A clinically significant reduction is defined as a 5-point drop from baseline.
qs.x: Correct: 30 of 40 CBI participants (75%) and 6 of 40 controls (15%) met the criterion, so RR = 0.75/0.15 = 5.0. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.20 inverts the ratio (control over CBI). B) 0.60 is the absolute risk difference (0.75 - 0.15), not a ratio. D) 17.0 is the odds ratio (30/10 divided by 6/34), not the relative risk. Trap: Reporting the absolute risk difference (0.60) or the odds ratio (17.0) instead of the ratio of the two proportions.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: The follow‑up period was relatively short.
Secondary outcomes showed improvement patterns similar to the primary outcome.
Participants who dropped out were excluded from the analysis.
qs.x: Correct: The passage never mentions dropouts or exclusions; it reports 40 participants per group and analyzes all of them. Why the others are wrong: A) the authors list a relatively short follow‑up period as a limitation. B) the authors list the absence of blinding as a limitation. C) the passage says secondary outcomes showed similar patterns of improvement. Trap: Assuming dropouts were handled because limitations are listed, when the passage never mentions them.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: The CBI eliminated anxiety symptoms in every treated participant.
More CBI than control participants dropped at least 5 points from baseline.
The effect of the CBI was shown to persist well beyond the 12‑week period.
The control group's mean anxiety score fell substantially over the 12 weeks.
qs.x: Correct: 30 of 40 CBI participants (75%) versus 6 of 40 controls (15%) met the response criterion. Why the others are wrong: A) only 30 of 40 participants responded and the post‑treatment mean (40.5) is still well above zero. C) the follow‑up period was short, so persistence was not tested. D) the control mean went from 50.4 to 52.0, a slight rise, not a fall. Trap: Treating a significant short-term group difference as proof of universal or lasting benefit.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of different auditory cues on cognitive performance during a sustained attention task. Twenty-four healthy adults (12 males, 12 females, age 22–35) were randomly assigned to one of four groups: Control (no cue), Condition A (continuous low‑frequency tone), Condition B (intermittent high‑frequency tone), and Condition C (continuous white noise). Each participant completed a 30‑minute vigilance task while their reaction times to target stimuli were recorded. The mean reaction time (RT) and standard deviation (SD) for each group are presented in Table 1. The researchers hypothesized that auditory cues would reduce RT variability, thereby improving sustained attention. Data analysis revealed that Condition A produced the fastest mean RT, followed by Condition C, Condition B, and the Control group. Despite the faster mean RT, Condition B exhibited the largest SD, suggesting increased inconsistency. The authors noted that the low‑frequency tone was associated with the fastest mean RT and the smallest SD, although no statistical test was reported, and they suggested future studies examine neural correlates using EEG.

qs.q: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time?
o: The control group's mean (350 ms) was higher than Condition A's 320 ms.
Condition B's mean was higher than Condition A's 320 ms, the lowest in the table.
Condition C's mean was higher than Condition A's 320 ms, the lowest in the table.
qs.x: The table shows Condition A had a mean RT of 320 ms, the lowest among all groups. Trap: Choosing the Control group or another condition without comparing all four means; the lowest mean reaction time is Condition A's 320 ms.

qs.q: Which factor was manipulated in this experiment?
o: Age wasn't changed by the researchers; it is a participant characteristic.
Gender mix is a sample characteristic, not something the researchers manipulated.
Task duration was the same for all groups, so it is a controlled variable.
qs.x: The independent variable was the type of auditory cue presented to participants. Trap: Mistaking participant characteristics or task length for the manipulated variable; only the auditory cue type was varied.

qs.q: What is the difference in mean reaction time between Condition A and the Control group?
o: 10 ms is too small; 350 − 320 is 30 ms.
20 ms doesn't match the two means of 350 and 320 ms.
40 ms is too large; the gap between 350 and 320 ms is 30 ms.
qs.x: 350 ms (Control) – 320 ms (Condition A) = 30 ms. Trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of means gives 10, 20 or 40 ms; the control minus Condition A is 350 − 320 = 30 ms.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid interpretation of the data?
o: Condition A had a lower mean RT than the Control group.
Condition B has the largest SD.
qs.x: Correct: B) Condition B had the largest SD (35 ms, versus 30 ms for Control), so its variability was higher, not lower. Why the others are wrong: A) 320 ms is lower than the Control mean of 350 ms. C) Condition C's SD (28 ms) is below the Control SD (30 ms). D) Condition B's SD of 35 ms is the largest of the four groups. Trap: Reading a larger SD as lower variability; a larger SD means more spread, so the claim that Condition B reduces variability is the misinterpretation.

qs.q: Which statement about Table 1 is supported by the data?
o: Every auditory cue condition had a lower mean RT than the Control group.
Every auditory cue condition had a lower SD than the Control group.
Condition B had the lowest mean RT of the three cue conditions.
Condition C had the largest SD of all four groups.
qs.x: Correct: Control mean RT was 350 ms, and Conditions A, B and C were 320, 340 and 330 ms, all lower. Why the others are wrong: B) Condition B had SD 35, higher than the Control SD of 30. C) Condition B (340 ms) had the highest mean RT of the three cue conditions, not the lowest. D) Condition B (SD 35) had the largest SD; Condition C was 28. Trap: Assuming every cue helped on every measure; Condition B had a higher SD than Control (35 vs 30 ms), so the claim that every condition lowered SD fails.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Weber described rationalization as the replacement of tradition and value judgment by calculated efficiency. Ritzer extended this as McDonaldization, characterized by efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control, often accompanied by the irrationality of rationality.
Observers studied four clinics adopting standardized protocols and recorded several measures (Table 1).

qs.q: Which dimension does a fixed visit length represent?
qs.x: Correct: Setting a numeric visit length emphasizes measurable quantity over qualitative judgment, which is calculability. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms belong to other frameworks. Trap: Calling any standardization efficiency.

qs.q: Which row illustrates the irrationality of rationality?
qs.x: Correct: The most efficient arrangement produced the worst patient experience, which is the outcome Ritzer calls the irrationality of rationality. Why the others are wrong: The baseline, navigator, and script-only rows do not show that reversal. Trap: Equating efficiency with improvement.

qs.q: What does the navigator row suggest?
qs.x: Correct: Adding a navigator kept visits short while restoring the share of addressed concerns, indicating the costs of standardization can be mitigated. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim conflicts with the row. Trap: Reading one unfavorable row as condemning the whole approach.

qs.q: Which dimension does a scripted intake represent?
qs.x: Correct: A standard script makes the encounter uniform across patients and staff. Why the others are wrong: The remaining dimensions concern quantity, substitution, and step reduction. Trap: Collapsing all four dimensions into efficiency.

qs.q: Which design feature limits these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Clinics chose which features to adopt, so differences may reflect the clinics rather than the protocols. Why the others are wrong: Site count limits generalization only, and the measures are appropriate. Trap: Listing a generalization limit as the main threat.

h: Share of patients reporting unaddressed concerns
r: Script, fixed length, and patient navigator

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Size-exclusion (gel filtration) chromatography separates molecules by size. Small molecules enter the pores of the beads and take a longer path, while large molecules are excluded and pass between beads, so they elute first. Ion-exchange chromatography separates by charge, and affinity chromatography uses a specific binding partner.
A protein mixture was run on a size-exclusion column calibrated with standards (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does thyroglobulin elute first?
o: It binds the beads most tightly
Size exclusion does not rely on binding.
It is the most positively charged
Charge is not the basis here.
It is too large to enter the pores
Correct: it takes the shortest path.
It is the smallest protein present
qs.x: Correct: Molecules larger than the pore size travel only in the space between beads, so they move through in the smallest volume. Why the others are wrong: Binding and charge are not the mechanism; it is the largest. Trap: Assuming big molecules are always retained longer.

qs.q: A protein elutes at 84 mL. What is its approximate mass?
qs.x: Correct: An elution volume of 84 mL falls between aldolase (158 kDa at 72 mL) and ovalbumin (44 kDa at 96 mL), so the mass is roughly 90 kDa. Why the others are wrong: Each corresponds to a different elution range. Trap: Reading the calibration backward.

qs.q: Why must the column be calibrated with standards?
o: Standards block the pores to improve resolution
Elution volume depends on the column
Correct: standards relate volume to mass.
qs.x: Correct: The relation between mass and elution volume depends on bead pore size, column dimensions and flow rate, so known proteins establish the curve. Why the others are wrong: Charge is irrelevant; standards do not block pores; calibration does not change mechanism. Trap: Thinking elution volume is an intrinsic property of the protein.

qs.q: Which technique would best isolate one protein from a complex mixture using a specific antibody?
o: Correct: a specific binding partner captures it.
qs.x: Correct: An immobilized antibody binds its target specifically, allowing other proteins to wash through. Why the others are wrong: The others separate by general physical properties rather than specific recognition. Trap: Choosing a high-resolution but nonspecific method.

qs.q: An elongated protein elutes earlier than a globular protein of the same mass. Why?
o: It binds the beads more weakly
Charge is not the basis here.
It is denser than the globular protein
qs.x: Correct: Size exclusion separates by hydrodynamic volume, and an extended shape sweeps out a larger volume than a compact one of equal mass, so it is excluded from pores sooner. Why the others are wrong: Charge, density and binding are not the separation basis. Trap: Treating molecular mass as the only determinant.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel small‑molecule inhibitor, Drug X, on the viability of cultured human cancer cells. Four concentrations of Drug X (0, 10, 50, and 100 µM) were applied to the cells for 48 hours. Cell viability was quantified using an MTT assay, and the results were expressed as a percentage of the untreated control. Each concentration was tested in ten replicate wells (n = 10). The investigators noted a dose‑dependent decrease in viability, with the highest concentration producing the greatest cytotoxic effect. Standard deviations increased slightly with concentration, suggesting greater variability at higher drug doses. The study aimed to determine whether Drug X could be a potential chemotherapeutic agent and to identify a concentration that maximizes efficacy while minimizing toxicity.

qs.q: What is the viability percentage of cells treated with 50 µM Drug X?
qs.x: The table shows that cells exposed to 50 µM of Drug X had a viability of 60%. Trap: Reading the wrong row, such as the 10 µM value (85%) or the 100 µM value (30%), instead of the 50 µM row.

qs.q: Which control group would best account for the solvent used to dissolve Drug X?
qs.x: A vehicle‑only control (e.g., DMSO without Drug X) controls for any effects of the solvent itself. Trap: Choosing untreated cells; they cannot separate solvent effects from drug effects, so a vehicle-only control is needed.

qs.q: Calculate the percent decrease in viability from 10 µM to 100 µM.
qs.x: Percent decrease = (85-30)/85 x 100 = 64.7%. The 55 is a drop of 55 percentage points, not a percent decrease relative to the 10 uM value. Trap: Reporting the 55 percentage-point drop (85-30) as the percent decrease instead of dividing by the starting value of 85.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: Drug X reduces viability at higher concentrations.
qs.x: The table shows viability at 100 µM is 30%, not 50%. The other statements are directly supported by the data. Trap: Assuming viability at 100 µM sits at the halfway point (50%) rather than reading the tabulated value of 30%.

qs.q: Which of the following is a potential clinical implication of these findings?
o: Drug X warrants further study as a chemotherapeutic.
Drug X is safe at high doses.
Drug X has no effect on cell viability.
qs.x: Correct: A) Dose-dependent loss of viability in cultured cancer cells justifies further study, though not clinical use. Why the others are wrong: B) Viability falls to 30% at 100 µM, which is toxicity, not safety. C) Viability falls with dose, so there is an effect. D) Viability decreases, the opposite of increased proliferation. Trap: Treating a cell-culture result as proof of safety or clinical use; the data show only dose-dependent cytotoxicity in vitro.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antimicrobial peptide (AMP) on the growth of Escherichia coli in a controlled in vitro assay. The experiment used a 96‑well plate with eight concentrations (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 µg/mL) and three replicates per concentration. After 24 hours of incubation at 37 °C, optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was measured. The data, summarized in Table 1, show a dose‑dependent decrease in bacterial growth, with the lowest OD observed at the highest peptide concentration. Additionally, the researchers performed a time‑kill assay at 32 µg/mL, recording CFU counts at 0, 2, 4, and 6 hours. The results indicated a 3‑log reduction after 4 hours. The study also examined the peptide’s cytotoxicity against mammalian cell lines, reporting an IC50 of 48 µg/mL. These findings describe the peptide’s antibacterial activity and its cytotoxicity at comparable concentrations.

qs.q: Which AMP concentration results in the greatest reduction in OD600 relative to the control (0 µg/mL)?
qs.x: The OD600 at 64 µg/mL (0.08) is the lowest among all concentrations, indicating the greatest reduction compared to the control (1.02). Trap: C (32 µg/mL) shows a substantial reduction but is not the lowest OD.

qs.q: Which experimental design element best supports a dose‑response relationship in this study?
o: A 96‑well plate, eight concentrations, three replicates each
Measuring OD600 after 24 hours of incubation
Performing a time‑kill assay at a single concentration
Assessing cytotoxicity against mammalian cell lines
qs.x: A 96‑well plate with multiple concentrations and replicates provides the necessary data points to establish a dose‑response curve. Trap: B (measuring OD600) is essential but does not alone establish dose‑response.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in OD600 at 32 µg/mL compared to the control?
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(1.02 – 0.15)/1.02] × 100 ≈ 85.3 %. Trap: Picking B (92.1%), which is roughly the reduction at 64 µg/mL (about 92%), the wrong concentration, instead of the 32 µg/mL value.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Higher AMP concentrations produce greater bacterial growth inhibition.
The peptide exhibits a 3‑log reduction in CFU after 4 hours at 32 µg/mL.
The mammalian IC50 (48 µg/mL) is below the time‑kill dose (32 µg/mL).
The OD600 values decrease in a dose‑dependent manner.
qs.x: Correct: C) 48 µg/mL is higher than 32 µg/mL, so the statement is false. Why the others are wrong: A) OD600 falls from 1.02 to 0.08 as concentration rises; supported. B) The passage reports a 3‑log reduction after 4 hours at 32 µg/mL; supported. D) OD600 decreases at every step in concentration; supported. Trap: Reading the IC50 of 48 µg/mL as lower than the 32 µg/mL used against bacteria; the mammalian IC50 is actually the higher number.

qs.q: Which statement best relates the antibacterial concentration to the mammalian cytotoxicity data?
o: The 32 µg/mL used in the time‑kill assay is below the mammalian IC50 of 48 µg/mL, but only by about 1.5‑fold, so the margin is narrow.
The mammalian IC50 of 48 µg/mL is lower than 32 µg/mL, so more than half of mammalian cells die at 32 µg/mL.
The dose‑dependent OD600 decrease shows the peptide is nontoxic to mammalian cells.
Because the IC50 is 48 µg/mL, the peptide is safe at every concentration tested in the OD600 assay.
qs.x: Correct: 48/32 = 1.5, so the time‑kill concentration is below the IC50 but not by a large factor. Why the others are wrong: B) 48 is higher than 32, not lower. C) OD600 was measured on E. coli and says nothing about mammalian cell toxicity. D) The assay went up to 64 µg/mL, which is above the IC50 of 48 µg/mL. Trap: Concluding that a peptide with a 3-log kill is automatically safe; the IC50 is only 1.5-fold above the concentration used against bacteria.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean OD600 values for E. coli exposed to AMP.

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder involves inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity beginning in childhood and causing impairment in more than one setting. Diagnosis requires symptoms across settings, which is why reports from both parents and teachers are collected. Stimulant medications increase dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in prefrontal circuits.
A clinic evaluated 200 referred children with ratings from two sources (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the diagnosis require symptoms in more than one setting?
o: Teachers are more accurate than parents
Two settings double the symptom count
Symptoms appear only at school in ADHD
qs.x: Correct: Difficulties confined to one setting often reflect that environment, such as a mismatched classroom or family stress, rather than a pervasive attentional disorder. Why the others are wrong: Counting is not the aim; neither informant is privileged; ADHD symptoms are pervasive. Trap: Treating multi-setting criteria as a way to gather more data.

qs.q: Why might parent and teacher ratings disagree?
o: Both can be accurate about their setting.
qs.x: Correct: A classroom requires sustained seated attention while home allows more movement, so the same child may appear impaired in one setting and not the other. Why the others are wrong: Both can be accurate; parallel forms exist; behavior varies. Trap: Assuming disagreement means error.

qs.q: Which neurotransmitters do stimulant medications mainly affect?
o: These are not the main targets.
These are targets of other drugs.
These are not the main targets.
qs.x: Correct: Stimulants block reuptake and promote release of dopamine and norepinephrine, improving prefrontal signal-to-noise. Why the others are wrong: Each names transmitters not primarily targeted. Trap: Choosing serotonin because it is prominent in other psychiatric drugs.

qs.q: Why is it notable that stimulants improve attention in children without ADHD too?
o: Drug response is not a test
Correct: treatment response is not a test.
It can still be clinically useful.
It shows stimulants do not work
qs.x: Correct: Because stimulants raise attention broadly, improvement on medication cannot be used as diagnostic evidence; diagnosis rests on symptom history and impairment. Why the others are wrong: Broad effects do not make everyone a case; the drugs work; medication can help. Trap: Using treatment response as a diagnostic test.

qs.q: Why do 12% of children rated high at school only still meet criteria?
o: Most such children did not meet criteria.
They were rated high at school.
qs.x: Correct: A parent may minimize or not observe difficulties, so a full evaluation including history and other sources can still establish cross-setting impairment in a minority of cases. Why the others are wrong: Criteria require more than one setting; symptoms were present; school ratings alone usually are not sufficient. Trap: Treating rating-scale patterns as the diagnosis itself.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antimicrobial peptide (AMP) on the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in vitro. Twenty-four bacterial cultures were inoculated in 96-well plates and exposed to AMP concentrations of 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 µg/mL for 24 hours. After incubation, optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was measured to assess bacterial growth. The results, summarized in Table 1, show a dose-dependent decrease in OD600, with complete inhibition observed at 32 µg/mL. In addition, the study measured the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) by serial dilution and determined the MIC to be 32 µg/mL. The researchers also performed time‑kill assays at each concentration; after 6 hours the reduction in colony‑forming units was 2.5 log at 8 µg/mL and 3.5 log at 32 µg/mL. Statistical analysis (ANOVA) indicated significant differences between concentrations (p < 0.01). The authors concluded that the AMP has potent antibacterial activity and could serve as a lead compound for new antibiotics.

qs.q: Which concentration shows the highest % inhibition?
qs.x: The table indicates that 32 µg/mL achieves 100% inhibition, the highest among the tested concentrations. Trap: The answer may be mistakenly chosen as 8 µg/mL because it shows a large inhibition (60%) but does not reach complete inhibition.

qs.q: Which experimental approach best determines the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the AMP?
o: A single OD600 reading at one AMP concentration
qs.x: Correct: C) The MIC is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it requires a series of (typically twofold) dilutions, each scored for growth. Why the others are wrong: A) one reading at a single concentration cannot locate the lowest inhibitory concentration. B) a time‑kill assay measures the rate and extent of killing (log CFU reduction) over time, not the growth-inhibition threshold. D) ANOVA tests differences between group means and does not define a concentration threshold. Trap: Choosing the time‑kill assay because it measures antibacterial activity, although it tracks killing over time rather than the lowest concentration that prevents growth.

qs.q: If the OD600 at 8 µg/mL is 0.40, what is the percent inhibition relative to the control?
qs.x: Percent inhibition = [(1.00 – 0.40)/1.00] × 100 = 60%. Trap: Some students may mistakenly use the OD600 of 0.70 (for 4 µg/mL) or miscalculate the subtraction.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: The AMP completely inhibits growth at 32 µg/mL.
The AMP shows a 2.5‑log reduction at 8 µg/mL after 6 hours.
qs.x: Correct: The table lists the OD600 at 0 µg/mL as 1.00, not 0.85 (0.85 is the value at 2 µg/mL). Why the others are wrong: A) the table shows 100% inhibition and OD600 of 0.00 at 32 µg/mL. B) the passage gives the MIC as 32 µg/mL, the lowest tested concentration with complete inhibition. C) the table and passage both report a 2.5‑log CFU reduction at 8 µg/mL at 6 h. Trap: Confusing the OD600 of the 2 µg/mL well (0.85) with the untreated control value (1.00).

qs.q: Which follow‑up experiment would best test whether the in vitro activity of the AMP is likely to translate into therapeutic benefit?
o: Repeating the same 24‑hour OD600 assay in the same medium and strain.
Measuring OD600 in wells that contain no bacteria.
Testing the AMP in an animal model of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.
qs.x: Correct: An animal infection model tests efficacy in a living host, which is the logical step after in vitro activity is shown. Why the others are wrong: A) repeating the same in vitro assay adds replication but no new information on efficacy in a host. B) wells without bacteria only provide a blank reading and say nothing about activity. D) the lowest concentrations had the least inhibition, so they add little about therapeutic potential. Trap: Choosing more in vitro replication because it feels rigorous, though it does not address efficacy in an infection.

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to attribute one's own behavior to situational factors while attributing the same behavior in others to disposition. It is thought to arise from differences in available information and in what is perceptually salient.
Participants explained both their own and a stranger's lateness, rudeness, and generosity, and each explanation was coded (Table 1).

qs.q: Which rows display the bias most clearly?
qs.x: Correct: The 47-point gap for lateness is the classic actor-observer pattern, whereas generosity shows almost none. Why the others are wrong: The generosity gap is small, and the remaining pairs hold target constant. Trap: Comparing rows that share the same target.

qs.q: Why is the generosity gap small?
qs.x: Correct: For favorable behavior people prefer dispositional self-explanations, which works against the usual actor-observer direction. Why the others are wrong: Situations do affect giving, information was matched, and definitions were standardized. Trap: Expecting the bias to be equally strong for all behaviors.

qs.q: Which added measure would test the information account?
qs.x: Correct: If the bias shrinks when observers report equal knowledge of the context, the information explanation gains support. Why the others are wrong: Duration, behavior count, and age do not index available information. Trap: Measuring effort instead of knowledge.

qs.q: Which bias overlaps with the generosity pattern?
qs.x: Correct: Taking dispositional credit for positive behavior is the self-serving bias. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms name different phenomena. Trap: Labeling every attribution pattern the fundamental attribution error.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of this design?
qs.x: Correct: Participants explained both targets without assignment, so order and selection effects cannot be excluded. Why the others are wrong: Behavior count, trained coding, and self-report are appropriate here. Trap: Criticizing a feature the design requires.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Simple distillation works when boiling points differ by more than about 25 °C. Fractional distillation uses a packed column in which repeated vaporization and condensation cycles enrich the vapor in the lower-boiling component. An azeotrope is a mixture whose vapor has the same composition as the liquid, so it cannot be separated further by distillation.
Students distilled a 50:50 mixture of ethanol (bp 78 °C) and water (bp 100 °C) and collected fractions (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does fractional distillation give a purer first fraction?
o: Water boils before ethanol in a column
The column heats the mixture more strongly
The column provides surface, not heat.
Correct: each cycle acts like another distillation.
qs.x: Correct: Vapor condenses and revaporizes many times on the packing, and each cycle enriches the vapor in the more volatile component, so the distillate is purer. Why the others are wrong: The column does not add heat or react; ethanol is more volatile. Trap: Thinking the column works by heating.

qs.q: Why can ethanol not be purified beyond about 95.6% this way?
o: It forms an azeotrope with water
Correct: vapor and liquid have the same composition.
Water is more volatile than ethanol
The column is not long enough in any apparatus
qs.x: Correct: At 95.6% ethanol the vapor has the same composition as the liquid, so further distillation gives no enrichment; other methods, such as adding a drying agent, are needed. Why the others are wrong: Ethanol is stable; no column can pass an azeotrope; ethanol is the more volatile component. Trap: Assuming a better column always gives more separation.

qs.q: Why does the head temperature rise during simple distillation?
o: The remaining liquid grows richer in water
Ethanol boils at a higher temperature later
The thermometer drifts upward over time
The heat source is turned up each minute
qs.x: Correct: As ethanol distills off, the pot liquid becomes more water rich, so its boiling point and the vapor temperature both rise. Why the others are wrong: The change is not from the heater or thermometer; pure component boiling points are fixed. Trap: Attributing the temperature rise to the apparatus.

qs.q: Which method would best separate two liquids boiling at 60 °C and 120 °C?
o: That is analytical, not preparative at this scale.
qs.x: Correct: With a 60 °C difference, simple distillation separates the components efficiently without the extra time and equipment of a column. Why the others are wrong: Fractional distillation is more than needed; recrystallization suits solids; TLC is analytical. Trap: Choosing the most powerful method rather than the appropriate one.

qs.q: Why is distillation done under reduced pressure for heat-sensitive compounds?
o: Lower pressure lowers the boiling point
Lower pressure raises the boiling point
qs.x: Correct: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals the external pressure, so reducing pressure allows distillation at a lower temperature and avoids decomposition. Why the others are wrong: Pressure reduction lowers boiling points and promotes vaporization; it is not a chemical process. Trap: Reversing the pressure-boiling point relation.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Culture includes material culture, such as objects and technology, and nonmaterial culture, such as values, beliefs, and norms. Cultural lag describes the delay between a material change and the normative adjustment that follows, and subcultures hold distinctive norms within a larger culture.
Researchers surveyed 2,500 adults about a newly common technology and the norms surrounding it (Table 1).

qs.q: Which concept do these results best illustrate?
qs.x: Correct: Widespread adoption with unsettled norms and frequent conflict is the gap between material and nonmaterial culture that cultural lag names. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms describe evaluative stances and group absorption. Trap: Describing any cultural change as lag without the timing contrast.

qs.q: Which item is material culture?
qs.x: Correct: Material culture consists of physical objects and technology. Why the others are wrong: Norms, interactions, and rules are nonmaterial. Trap: Counting written rules as material because they are recorded.

qs.q: What does the subculture figure add?
qs.x: Correct: A small minority occupies a setting with formal rules, showing normative adjustment proceeding faster in some groups than others. Why the others are wrong: Rejection was not measured, norms are not shared, and ownership was high. Trap: Treating a subculture figure as a measure of resistance.

qs.q: Which figure shows the clearest normative gap?
qs.x: Correct: The contrast between high ownership and low norm clarity measures the gap directly. Why the others are wrong: Conflict is downstream, the subculture figure is narrow, and ownership alone is one side. Trap: Choosing the consequence instead of the gap.

qs.q: Which added measure would show lag closing?
qs.x: Correct: Tracking reported norm clarity across years would show whether nonmaterial culture catches up with the material change. Why the others are wrong: Price, model variety, and cross-national ownership do not measure norms. Trap: Tracking the technology instead of the norms.

r: Share reporting clear norms for its use in meetings
Share reporting conflict over its use at family meals
Share in a professional subculture with written rules

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Reaction rates rise with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT). Enzymes also follow this trend until heat denatures them, so enzyme activity shows an optimum temperature and falls sharply above it. Denaturation is a loss of three-dimensional structure, not of covalent bonds in the backbone.
Students measured the initial rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction and of the same uncatalyzed reaction at several temperatures (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the enzyme-catalyzed rate fall above 40 °C while the uncatalyzed rate keeps rising?
o: Eₐ is a property of the pathway.
Collisions become less frequent when hot
qs.x: Correct: Above the optimum, the enzyme's folded structure unravels, so fewer functional active sites remain and the rate falls even though molecular motion increases. Why the others are wrong: The substrate survives; Eₐ does not change with temperature; collisions increase. Trap: Expecting the Arrhenius trend to hold without limit for enzymes.

qs.q: By what factor does the uncatalyzed rate rise from 20 °C to 40 °C?
qs.x: Correct: The rate doubles per 10 °C here, so over 20 °C it rises fourfold from 0.002 to 0.008 μmol/min. Why the others are wrong: 2 covers one interval; 20 is a temperature span; 41 is the catalyzed value. Trap: Reading across to the wrong column.

qs.q: How does an enzyme increase the reaction rate?
o: Enzymes do not heat the solution.
Concentration is set by the experiment.
qs.x: Correct: By stabilizing the transition state, an enzyme lowers Eₐ, so a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy at any temperature. Why the others are wrong: Enzymes do not heat solutions, change ΔG or create substrate. Trap: Thinking catalysis makes a reaction more thermodynamically favorable.

qs.q: What does denaturation change in a protein?
o: The number of amino acids present
qs.x: Correct: Denaturation disrupts the noncovalent interactions and disulfides that hold the tertiary structure, while the primary sequence remains. Why the others are wrong: The sequence, residue count and gene are unchanged. Trap: Equating denaturation with hydrolysis.

qs.q: Why do enzymes from hot-spring bacteria work at 80 °C?
o: They do not lower activation energy
They have no tertiary structure to lose
More stabilizing interactions in their structures
They use different amino acids not found elsewhere
qs.x: Correct: Thermophilic enzymes have extra ion pairs, tighter packing and other features that raise their denaturation temperature, so their optimum shifts upward. Why the others are wrong: They are folded; they use standard amino acids; they catalyze in the usual way. Trap: Assuming a different chemistry rather than greater stability.

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Stereotype threat is the performance decrement that occurs when a person fears confirming a negative stereotype about their group. It is thought to act by consuming working memory with monitoring and anxiety, and it can be reduced by altering how a task is framed.
Students completed a difficult quantitative test under randomly assigned framings, and working memory load was measured concurrently (Table 1).

qs.q: Which result supports the working memory account?
qs.x: Correct: Conditions with higher measured load produced lower scores, consistent with threat occupying capacity needed for the test. Why the others are wrong: Overall score level, condition count, and the direction of the affirmation effect do not support the claim. Trap: Reading any score difference as mechanism evidence.

qs.q: Why does the puzzle framing help?
qs.x: Correct: Removing the claim that the test measures ability removes the stereotype-relevant evaluation. Why the others are wrong: Items and timing were identical, and framing did change the load index. Trap: Attributing the gain to task difficulty.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the threat account?
o: Load fell but scores stayed low
qs.x: Correct: If reducing load left performance unchanged, the proposed mediating pathway would be undermined. Why the others are wrong: The remaining results are predictions or assumptions of the account. Trap: Treating a confirmatory result as a challenge.

qs.q: What was randomly assigned here?
qs.x: Correct: Only the framing of the test was assigned by the researchers. Why the others are wrong: Group membership, items, and the load measure were fixed. Trap: Assuming group identity can be randomized.

qs.q: Which practical implication follows?
qs.x: Correct: Presenting assessments as opportunities to solve problems rather than as measures of fixed ability reduced the decrement. Why the others are wrong: Difficulty and timing were not manipulated, and separating groups would raise identity salience. Trap: Recommending a change the study did not test.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antibiotic on the growth of *Staphylococcus aureus* in vitro. The experiment involved culturing the bacteria in a nutrient broth and adding the antibiotic at a single concentration (5 µg/mL). Samples were taken just before the antibiotic was added (Day 0) and at 1, 3, 5, and 7 days post-treatment. Bacterial counts were measured by serial dilution and plating, and the antibiotic concentration was confirmed by high-performance liquid chromatography. The goal was to describe the time-dependent bactericidal activity at that concentration; the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was not determined. The data collected provide insights into both the potency and the kinetics of bacterial killing, which are critical for informing dosing regimens in clinical settings. The researchers plan to use these findings to design subsequent in vivo studies and to evaluate potential resistance mechanisms.

qs.q: Based on the table, which day shows the highest bacterial count?
qs.x: Correct: Day 0 has 1.2×10⁶ CFU/mL, the highest count, and no antibiotic is present yet (0 µg/mL). Why the others are wrong: B) Day 1 is 8.5×10⁵ CFU/mL, lower than Day 0. C) Day 3 is 3.1×10⁵ CFU/mL, lower. D) Day 5 is 1.0×10⁴ CFU/mL, far lower. Trap: Picking a later day by assuming bacteria keep multiplying in broth over time, ignoring that counts fell after the antibiotic was added on Day 0.

qs.q: Which experimental control would best determine whether the observed bacterial killing is due to the antibiotic rather than other variables?
o: A culture with no antibiotic added
A culture with a known ineffective antibiotic
A culture with vancomycin at the same concentration
A culture with the antibiotic but no bacteria
qs.x: A culture with no antibiotic serves as a negative control, showing bacterial growth in the absence of treatment. This allows comparison to antibiotic-treated cultures to attribute effects specifically to the drug. Trap: Option B is tempting because it introduces another antibiotic, but it does not isolate the effect of the novel drug.

qs.q: Calculate the percent reduction in bacterial count from Day 0 to Day 5.
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(1.2×10⁶ – 1.0×10⁴) / 1.2×10⁶] × 100 ≈ 99.2%. The calculation uses the baseline and Day 5 counts. Trap: Using the wrong time point or denominator; for example, the fall to Day 3 is only 74.2%, whereas the fall to Day 5 relative to the Day 0 count is 99.2%.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is best supported by the data in Table 1?
o: The antibiotic is bacteriostatic because bacterial counts never return to baseline.
The MIC is 5 µg/mL since no growth is seen after Day 5.
The antibiotic kills all bacteria within 3 days.
No bacteria were recovered at Day 7, consistent with bactericidal activity at 5 µg/mL.
qs.x: CFU/mL fell from 1.2×10⁶ at Day 0 to 0 at Day 7 at a constant 5 µg/mL, consistent with bactericidal killing. Counts were still 3.1×10⁵ at Day 3, so killing was not complete within 3 days; a single concentration cannot define an MIC; and a progressive fall to zero is not bacteriostatic behavior. Trap: Option B is tempting because the concentration is constant, but an MIC requires testing multiple concentrations, and Day 5 still shows 1.0×10⁴ CFU/mL, so 'no growth after Day 5' is wrong.

qs.q: Table 1 tests only one antibiotic concentration (5 µg/mL). Which additional experiment would be needed to determine the MIC of the antibiotic?
o: Finding the lowest antibiotic concentration that prevents visible growth
Counting bacteria at more time points while keeping the concentration at 5 µg/mL
Measuring bacterial counts at Day 7 only
Adding vancomycin to the cultures treated with 5 µg/mL
qs.x: Correct: The MIC is by definition the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it requires testing several concentrations. Why the others are wrong: B) more time points at one concentration describe kinetics, not the lowest inhibitory concentration. C) a Day 7 count at one concentration cannot compare concentrations. D) adding a second drug confounds the result and does not define the MIC of the novel drug. Trap: Treating the Day 7 count of zero at 5 µg/mL as the MIC, although only one concentration was tested.

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Conformity is a change in behavior to match a group. Asch's line-judgment studies found that many participants gave an obviously wrong answer when confederates did so first. Normative influence is conformity to be accepted; informational influence is conformity because others are believed to be right. Conformity falls sharply when even one other person dissents.
Participants judged which comparison line matched a standard, in groups where confederates gave wrong answers (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does one dissenting confederate reduce conformity so much?
o: Correct: the pressure to agree falls.
qs.x: Correct: A single ally shows that disagreement is possible and removes the sense that one would stand alone, which cuts conforming errors from 34% to 6%. Why the others are wrong: The task, group size and order are unchanged. Trap: Attributing the drop to a change in task difficulty.

qs.q: Why does private responding reduce conformity but not eliminate it?
o: Conformity requires no social context at all
Correct: others may still seem right.
Participants cannot see the lines privately
qs.x: Correct: Writing answers privately removes the fear of disapproval, but some participants still believe the majority must be perceiving something they missed. Why the others are wrong: Vision and recording are unaffected; social context matters. Trap: Treating conformity as entirely about being seen.

qs.q: What distinguishes normative from informational influence?
o: Both involve only private belief change
qs.x: Correct: Normative influence produces public compliance to gain approval, while informational influence produces private acceptance because others are taken as a guide to reality. Why the others are wrong: Each misstates one of the two. Trap: Swapping the definitions.

qs.q: Why did the control condition use participants judging alone?
o: It increases the number of trials
Trial count is not the aim.
It shows the task is easy
qs.x: Correct: With a 1% baseline error rate, the 34% error rate in groups cannot be explained by perceptual difficulty and must reflect social influence. Why the others are wrong: Acuity and trial count are not the point; conformity did occur. Trap: Dismissing a control as unnecessary.

qs.q: Why would conformity differ between cultures?
o: Only one culture has been studied
qs.x: Correct: Replications find higher conformity in cultures that emphasize group cohesion, consistent with normative influence being shaped by social values. Why the others are wrong: Perception is comparable; conformity varies with context; many cultures have been studied. Trap: Looking for a perceptual rather than a normative explanation.

r: Six confederates, one gives the correct answer

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Le Châtelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change. Adding a reactant shifts the system toward products; removing a product shifts it the same way. Raising temperature shifts an endothermic reaction toward products. Changing pressure shifts gas equilibria toward the side with fewer moles of gas. A catalyst changes neither position nor K.
Students studied the equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), where N₂O₄ is colorless and NO₂ is brown, and ΔH = +57 kJ/mol (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does heating shift the equilibrium toward NO₂?
o: NO₂ is more stable at all temperatures
Heating always favors the gas with fewer moles
qs.x: Correct: Because the forward reaction is endothermic, adding heat is like adding a reactant, so the system shifts toward products. Why the others are wrong: ΔH is positive; mole counts relate to pressure; relative stability varies with temperature. Trap: Mixing up endothermic and exothermic responses.

qs.q: Why does compressing the syringe ultimately lighten the color?
o: Compression removes NO₂ from the tube
qs.x: Correct: Halving the volume first concentrates NO₂, darkening the color, but the system then shifts toward N₂O₄, which has fewer moles of gas, so the color lightens relative to the initial jump. Why the others are wrong: The system is closed; pressure rises; concentration matters. Trap: Reading only the instantaneous change.

qs.q: Why does a catalyst not shift the equilibrium?
o: It changes ΔH of the reaction
It is consumed by the reaction
qs.x: Correct: A catalyst lowers the activation barrier for forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so equilibrium is reached faster at the same position. Why the others are wrong: Catalysts are not consumed, do not change ΔH, and act in many phases. Trap: Assuming faster means further.

qs.q: How would adding an inert gas at constant volume affect this equilibrium?
o: A shift toward N₂O₄, since total pressure rises
No shift, since partial pressures are unchanged
A shift toward NO₂, since pressure rises
Partial pressures of the reactants do not change.
qs.x: Correct: At constant volume, adding an inert gas raises total pressure but leaves the partial pressures and concentrations of N₂O₄ and NO₂ unchanged, so no shift occurs. Why the others are wrong: Partial pressures determine the shift; the reaction continues. Trap: Using total pressure instead of partial pressures.

qs.q: What happens to the value of K when the temperature is raised?
o: Product formation does not lower K here.
K stays the same at all temperatures
qs.x: Correct: K is temperature dependent; for an endothermic reaction, raising temperature increases K. Why the others are wrong: Concentration changes do not alter K; K varies with temperature and stays finite. Trap: Treating K as a universal constant.

r: Sealed tube placed in hot water
Sealed tube placed in ice water

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Prejudice is an attitude, discrimination is behavior, and stereotypes are beliefs about group attributes. Implicit measures such as reaction-time association tasks are thought to capture automatic associations that may diverge from explicitly reported attitudes.
Researchers measured explicit attitudes, an implicit association score, and two behaviors in 800 adults (Table 1).

qs.q: What pattern do these correlations show?
qs.x: Correct: Explicit attitudes predicted deliberate, controllable responses while implicit scores predicted spontaneous nonverbal behavior, a well-documented double dissociation. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim contradicts part of the table. Trap: Ranking the two measures instead of matching them to behavior type.

qs.q: Which outcome is behavioral discrimination?
qs.x: Correct: Seating distance is an observable behavior toward a member of the group. Why the others are wrong: The remaining measures capture attitudes, associations, or beliefs. Trap: Treating a stated intention as behavior.

qs.q: Which criticism of implicit measures do these data not address?
qs.x: Correct: Stability over repeated administrations is a central criticism that a single measurement cannot evaluate. Why the others are wrong: The remaining criticisms are addressed by the table. Trap: Choosing a criticism the data do speak to.

qs.q: Which correlation is strongest overall?
qs.x: Correct: The explicit attitude correlated 0.61 with reported willingness to befriend. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining correlation is smaller. Trap: Assuming the implicit measure must lead because it is less transparent.

qs.q: Which design change would permit causal claims?
qs.x: Correct: Experimentally altering automatic associations and observing behavior change would support a causal interpretation. Why the others are wrong: More outcomes, more participants, and repeated measurement remain correlational. Trap: Treating a bigger correlational study as causal evidence.

r: Seating distance chosen in a waiting room
Hiring recommendation on a rated form
Duration of eye contact during conversation

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Milgram's obedience studies examined compliance with an authority's instructions to deliver increasing shocks to a learner. Obedience was high when the authority was present and legitimate, and fell when the authority was remote, when the victim was close, or when other participants refused. Obedience reflects situational pressures rather than unusual personal cruelty.
Table 1 summarizes obedience rates across variations.

qs.q: Which factor most reduced obedience in these variations?
qs.x: Correct: Seeing peers refuse dropped full obedience to 10%, the lowest rate among these variations. Why the others are wrong: Each reduced obedience less. Trap: Assuming physical proximity to the victim matters most.

qs.q: What do these variations suggest about the cause of obedience?
qs.x: Correct: The same kinds of participants obeyed 65% of the time in one arrangement and 10% in another, which locates the cause in the situation rather than in character. Why the others are wrong: Cruelty and personality cannot explain the variation; the studies were experimental. Trap: Explaining behavior by disposition when the situation varied.

qs.q: Why does the presence of a legitimate authority increase obedience?
o: Participants did not understand the task
qs.x: Correct: Milgram described an agentic state in which people see themselves as carrying out another's will and no longer feel personally responsible. Why the others are wrong: Participants were distressed; no force was used; the task was understood. Trap: Assuming compliance implies enjoyment.

qs.q: Why are these studies difficult to run today?
o: Correct: deception and distress are limited.
Volunteering is not the main obstacle.
The results are no longer of interest
qs.x: Correct: Modern review boards require informed consent, the right to withdraw and protection from severe psychological distress, which the original design did not provide. Why the others are wrong: The topic remains important; equipment and volunteering are not the barriers. Trap: Explaining the change in practice by practical rather than ethical reasons.

qs.q: Why is the nonauthority condition informative?
o: It shows no one obeys instructions
qs.x: Correct: The same instructions from someone without authority produced far less obedience, which shows that perceived legitimacy carries much of the effect. Why the others are wrong: Some still obeyed; authority clearly mattered; distress was not measured. Trap: Reading a reduced rate as no effect.

h: Share continuing to the maximum shock
r: Baseline, authority present, victim in another room
Ordinary person, not an authority, gives orders

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Social facilitation describes improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks when others are present, and impaired performance on complex or novel tasks. Zajonc explained this by arousal, which strengthens dominant responses. Social loafing, in contrast, is reduced individual effort when contributions are pooled and not identifiable.
Participants completed two tasks alone or before an audience (Table 1). Scores are percent correct.

qs.q: Why does an audience help typing but hurt the logic puzzle?
o: Correct: helpful when correct, harmful when not.
qs.x: Correct: Arousal makes the most readily available response more likely; for a well-learned skill that response is usually correct, while for a novel task it is often wrong. Why the others are wrong: Typing improved; puzzles need attention; arousal can impair. Trap: Treating audience effects as uniformly positive or negative.

qs.q: How does social loafing differ from social facilitation?
o: It occurs when effort is hidden.
It occurs only on simple tasks
qs.x: Correct: Social facilitation concerns the effect of being observed on performance, while social loafing concerns reduced effort when individual contributions cannot be identified within a group product. Why the others are wrong: It is not task limited; effort falls; being unobserved is the key. Trap: Confusing the two group effects.

qs.q: Why would a practiced musician perform better in front of a crowd?
o: Audiences have no effect on skilled performers
Correct: arousal aids the dominant response.
Practice is what makes the skill dominant.
qs.x: Correct: For a thoroughly practiced piece, the dominant response is the correct one, so added arousal improves execution. Why the others are wrong: Crowds raise arousal; practice matters; audiences do affect performers. Trap: Assuming expertise removes audience effects.

qs.q: How could the logic puzzle result be reduced in a workplace?
o: Require the task to be done in public first
Early public performance is when impairment occurs.
Add more observers to the room
qs.x: Correct: Practicing until the correct response is dominant means that any arousal from observation enhances rather than disrupts performance. Why the others are wrong: Each adds arousal during the novel phase. Trap: Trying to raise motivation when the problem is excess arousal.

qs.q: Why is it important that the logic puzzle was novel?
qs.x: Correct: Social facilitation theory predicts impairment specifically when the dominant response is not the correct one, which is characteristic of unpracticed tasks. Why the others are wrong: Scoring occurred; arousal remains; the task was harder. Trap: Overlooking why task familiarity is the critical variable.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the cytotoxic effects of a novel chemotherapeutic agent on a human breast cancer cell line. Cells were exposed to varying concentrations of the drug (0, 10, 20, 40, and 80 µM) for 48 hours, after which cell viability was assessed using an MTT assay. The results, expressed as a percentage of the untreated control, are summarized in Table 1. The standard deviation for each concentration reflects the variability observed across three independent experiments. The data suggest a dose‑dependent decrease in viability, with the highest concentration (80 µM) reducing viability to 20 % of the control. These findings support further investigation of the drug’s therapeutic potential and warrant additional studies to elucidate its mechanism of action.

qs.q: What is the cell viability at a drug concentration of 20 µM?
qs.x: The table shows that at 20 µM the viability is 70 % of the untreated control. Trap: Option A (45 %) corresponds to the 40 µM concentration, which could mislead readers who overlook the concentration‑viability pairing.

qs.q: Which control would best distinguish an effect of the drug from an effect of the solvent used to dissolve it?
o: A vehicle control containing the solvent used to dissolve the drug.
A positive control using a known cytotoxic agent.
A negative control with no cells.
A time‑zero control measuring viability immediately after drug addition.
qs.x: Correct: A) A vehicle control receives the solvent alone, so any change in viability beyond it is due to the drug. Why the others are wrong: B) A positive control checks that the assay can detect cytotoxicity but does not separate drug from solvent. C) A no-cell blank corrects background absorbance. D) A time-zero control sets the starting viability, not the solvent effect. Trap: Choosing a positive control because it validates the assay, even though only a vehicle-only control isolates the solvent effect.

qs.q: What is the percent decrease in viability from the control to the 80 µM concentration?
qs.x: The control is 100 %. At 80 µM viability is 20 %, so the decrease is 100 % – 20 % = 80 %. Trap: Option B (50 %) might be chosen by students who mistakenly calculate the difference between 70 % (20 µM) and 20 % (80 µM) instead of comparing to the control.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is FALSE?
o: The viability decreases as drug concentration increases.
The standard deviation increases with higher drug concentrations.
The 10 µM concentration shows a lower viability than the 20 µM concentration.
The 0 µM concentration serves as the control and is set to 100 % viability.
qs.x: Viability falls with dose (100, 85, 70, 45, 20 %) and the SD rises monotonically (2, 3, 4, 5, 6), so A, B and D are true. C is false because 10 µM (85 %) has higher, not lower, viability than 20 µM (70 %). Trap: Option B looks suspicious because of the word 'increases', but the SD does increase at every step (2 to 6).

qs.q: Assuming viability falls linearly between the 20 µM and 40 µM points, at about what concentration would viability be 50% of control?
qs.x: Correct: C) Between 20 and 40 µM viability falls from 70% to 45%, or 1.25 percentage points per µM; dropping from 70% to 50% needs 16 µM, so about 36 µM. Why the others are wrong: A) 25 µM would give about 64%. B) 30 µM would give about 58%. D) 40 µM gives 45%, which is below 50%. Trap: Picking 40 µM because 45% is the closest tabulated value, without interpolating between the 20 and 40 µM points.
