passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Social capital refers to resources available through social relationships. Bonding capital links similar people and supplies support, while bridging capital links different groups and supplies access. Communities with higher social capital often show better collective outcomes.
Investigators followed 90 neighborhoods for five years, measuring capital indicators and outcomes (Table 1).

qs.q: Which capital type best predicts employment gains here?
qs.x: Correct: Employment rose most in neighborhoods with high bridging capital, consistent with access to outside opportunity. Why the others are wrong: Bonding alone produced little gain, and the two types differ in effect. Trap: Assuming close community ties drive economic opportunity.

qs.q: What does bonding capital typically supply?
qs.x: Correct: Bonding capital provides solidarity and support among similar people. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options describe bridging, authority, and economic capital. Trap: Treating all social ties as interchangeable resources.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects causal claims?
qs.x: Correct: Neighborhoods were classified rather than assigned, so prior differences could drive both capital levels and employment change. Why the others are wrong: The remaining features are strengths. Trap: Treating a cohort design as experimental.

qs.q: Which type lost employment?
qs.x: Correct: Neighborhoods low on both measures were the only group to decline. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining type gained. Trap: Misreading the sign of the smallest gain.

qs.q: Which added measure would clarify the pathway?
qs.x: Correct: If bridging capital works by supplying access to opportunity, measuring referrals tests that pathway directly. Why the others are wrong: Population size, tenure, and prices do not measure access. Trap: Adding outcomes rather than the proposed mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Environmental justice concerns the unequal distribution of environmental hazards and benefits across social groups. Studies examine siting of polluting facilities, exposure levels, and whether disparities arise from siting decisions or from subsequent movement of residents.
Researchers examined 300 census tracts near industrial facilities (Table 1).

qs.q: What do these columns together show?
qs.x: Correct: Particulate exposure rises steadily with the share of low-income residents, which is the disparity environmental justice research describes. Why the others are wrong: The distribution is graded, the income direction is implausible, and most facilities are recent. Trap: Treating a graded disparity as random variation.

qs.q: Which question does the siting column help answer?
qs.x: Correct: Knowing when facilities were built addresses whether hazards were placed in already low-income areas or whether residents moved in afterward. Why the others are wrong: Harm, income accuracy, and comparability are different questions. Trap: Reading a timing variable as an exposure measure.

qs.q: Which design would best resolve the siting debate?
o: Finer exposure data do not help.
qs.x: Correct: Following neighborhood composition from before each facility was built distinguishes discriminatory siting from subsequent residential change. Why the others are wrong: More tracts, finer exposure data, and current surveys leave the timing unresolved. Trap: Improving exposure measurement when the question concerns sequence.

qs.q: Which quartile has the highest low-income share?
qs.x: Correct: The most exposed tracts have the largest share of low-income residents. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining quartile is lower. Trap: Reading the exposure column.

qs.q: Which added measure would link exposure to health?
qs.x: Correct: Health outcome data are needed to connect the documented exposure disparity to consequences for residents. Why the others are wrong: Facility counts, area, and rent do not measure health. Trap: Adding exposure detail instead of outcomes.

h: Mean annual particulate exposure, micrograms per cubic metre
Share of residents in the lowest income quartile

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: The demographic transition describes movement from high birth and death rates to low ones. Stage one has both high, stage two has falling deaths with births still high and rapid growth, stage three has falling births, and stage four has both low.
Researchers compiled vital statistics for four countries (Table 1).

qs.q: Which country is in stage two?
qs.x: Correct: Stage two is marked by mortality decline while fertility remains high, producing the fastest growth. Why the others are wrong: The remaining countries show both rates high, falling births, or both low. Trap: Assigning stage by growth rate alone.

qs.q: Which country shows the smallest natural increase?
qs.x: Correct: Natural increase is births minus deaths, which is only one per thousand in Country Z. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining country has a larger gap. Trap: Using the growth rate column, which also includes migration.

qs.q: Why can the growth rate differ from natural increase?
qs.x: Correct: Population growth combines natural increase with net migration, so the two columns need not match. Why the others are wrong: No counting or reporting problems were described, and the rates are current. Trap: Treating growth rate and natural increase as the same quantity.

qs.q: What characterizes stage four?
qs.x: Correct: In stage four birth and death rates are both low and population growth is minimal. Why the others are wrong: The remaining descriptions name earlier stages. Trap: Assuming stage four means population decline.

qs.q: Which additional measure would most improve stage assignment?
qs.x: Correct: The total fertility rate adjusts for age structure and so classifies fertility behavior more reliably than the crude birth rate. Why the others are wrong: Size, area, and income are not fertility measures. Trap: Using population size as a demographic stage indicator.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of varying environmental parameters on the growth rate of a marine bacterium, *Pseudoalteromonas marina*. The experiment was conducted in triplicate using a controlled incubator. In the control group, the temperature was maintained at 22 °C, the pH at 7.8, the nutrient concentration at 0.5 g L⁻¹, and the incubation time was 48 h. In the experimental group, the temperature was increased to 28 °C, the pH was lowered to 6.5, the nutrient concentration was doubled to 1.0 g L⁻¹, and the incubation time was extended to 72 h. At the end of incubation, bacterial density was measured using optical density at 600 nm. The control group exhibited an optical density of 0.45, whereas the experimental group reached 1.20. The researchers concluded that the combined changes in temperature, pH, nutrient concentration, and time together increased bacterial growth.

qs.q: Based on the data presented, which environmental parameter showed the greatest percent change relative to its control value?
qs.x: Correct: C) Nutrient concentration doubled from 0.5 to 1.0 g/L, a 100% increase. Why the others are wrong: A) Temperature rose 6 °C from 22 °C, about 27%. B) pH fell 1.3 from 7.8, about 17%. D) Incubation time rose 24 h from 48 h, 50%. Trap: Comparing raw differences across different units (24 h versus 6 °C versus 1.3 pH units) makes incubation time look largest; percent change relative to control puts them on one scale.

qs.q: Which modification to the experimental design would most directly test whether temperature alone is responsible for the observed increase in bacterial growth?
o: Include a second experimental group with temperature 28 °C but pH 7.8, nutrient concentration 0.5 g L⁻¹, and time 48 h.
Add a third group with temperature 22 °C, pH 6.5, nutrient concentration 1.0 g L⁻¹, and time 72 h.
This changes temperature, pH, nutrients and time all at once, so no single cause can be identified.
Run the experiment with temperature 28 °C, pH 6.5, nutrient concentration 1.0 g L⁻¹, but time 48 h.
This changes temperature and also pH and nutrients, so temperature's effect can't be separated out.
Repeat the original experiment but measure growth at 24 h intervals.
Measuring more often adds detail but doesn't separate temperature from the other variables.
qs.x: Group A isolates temperature as the variable by keeping all other parameters at control levels, allowing assessment of temperature’s independent effect. Trap: Option C is tempting because it keeps temperature high, but it still changes time, confounding the effect.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in optical density from the control to the experimental group.
o: 200% would mean OD tripled to 1.35, not 1.20.
267% comes from dividing 1.20 by 0.45 without subtracting the baseline first.
qs.x: Percent increase = (1.20 − 0.45)/0.45 × 100 = 166.7 % ≈ 167 %. Trap: Students sometimes subtract the control from the experimental and then divide by the experimental value, yielding an incorrect 63 %.

qs.q: What is the approximate change in hydrogen ion concentration between the control (pH 7.8) and experimental (pH 6.5) conditions?
qs.x: Correct: B) [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so the ratio is 10^(7.8 - 6.5) = 10¹.3, about 20-fold higher at pH 6.5. Why the others are wrong: A) This treats the 1.3-unit pH difference as a fold change. C) 13 comes from multiplying 10 by 1.3 rather than raising 10 to the 1.3 power. D) 1.2 is the ratio 7.8/6.5 of the pH numbers, which ignores the logarithmic scale. Trap: Treating pH as a linear scale, so a 1.3-unit change is read as a 1.3-fold (or 1.2-fold) change in hydrogen ion concentration.

qs.q: Which conclusion is supported by the data and design described?
o: Density was higher in the experimental (OD 1.20) than control (0.45).
Raising the temperature to 28 °C alone increased bacterial growth.
The four changed parameters were shown to act synergistically.
Lowering the pH to 6.5 reduced bacterial growth.
qs.x: Correct: A) The measured optical densities were 1.20 (experimental) and 0.45 (control). Why the others are wrong: B) All four parameters changed together, so temperature alone cannot be credited. C) Synergy would need single-factor and combined groups to compare; none were run. D) The experimental group, which had the lower pH, grew more, and pH was not varied alone. Trap: Attributing the growth increase to one parameter or to synergy, even though all four parameters changed at once and no single-factor groups were run.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers investigated the antibacterial activity of a novel amphipathic peptide, designated AP‑42, against *Escherichia coli* cultured under controlled laboratory conditions. The study employed a factorial design with two independent variables: peptide concentration (0, 5, 10, 20, 40 µg/mL) and medium pH (5.5, 7.0, 8.5). For each treatment combination, bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm (OD600) over a 24‑hour period, and the maximum specific growth rate (μmax) was calculated from the exponential phase. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate a dose‑dependent inhibition of growth at neutral and alkaline pH, whereas acidic pH attenuates the peptide’s efficacy. The authors concluded that AP‑42 exhibits potent antibacterial activity, particularly at pH 7.0 and 8.5, and suggested its potential as a therapeutic agent for infections in body sites with neutral to slightly alkaline pH. The data also raise questions about the peptide’s mechanism of action and its stability across pH ranges.

qs.q: Which peptide concentration at pH 7.0 produced the lowest μmax?
o: 5 µg/mL gave a higher μmax than 40 µg/mL; growth falls as concentration rises.
10 µg/mL still allowed more growth than the highest concentration.
20 µg/mL gave a higher μmax than 40 µg/mL.
qs.x: At pH 7.0 the μmax values decrease with increasing peptide concentration. The lowest μmax (0.15 h⁻¹) occurs at the highest concentration tested, 40 µg/mL. Trap: Option C (20 µg/mL) is tempting because it also shows a marked reduction, but it is not the lowest.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
o: No participants were randomized to treatment and control arms in a clinical sense; two factors were varied in combination.
A cohort study follows a group over time without manipulating variables.
A case-control study compares groups chosen by outcome, which isn't what was done here.
qs.x: The investigators varied two independent variables (peptide concentration and pH) simultaneously and measured the outcome for each combination, which is the hallmark of a factorial design. Trap: Option A is plausible because the study involved controlled conditions, but it is not a randomized trial.

qs.q: If the μmax at 10 µg/mL and pH 7.0 is 0.45 h⁻¹, what is the percent reduction in μmax compared to the control (0 µg/mL) at the same pH, given the control μmax is 1.20 h⁻¹?
o: 25% would leave a μmax of 0.90 h⁻¹, not 0.45.
37.5% is the fraction remaining (0.45 ÷ 1.20), not the reduction.
qs.x: Reduction = (1.20 – 0.45)/1.20 = 0.75/1.20 = 0.625 = 62.5%. Trap: Option C (50%) is a common mis‑calculation if the difference is divided by the treated value instead of the control.

qs.q: Which statement is most likely incorrect regarding the peptide’s activity?
o: Activity is enhanced at higher pH
This is consistent with the data: the peptide works better at higher pH.
Activity is reduced at acidic pH
This is consistent with the data: acidic pH reduces activity.
This is consistent with the data: more peptide means more inhibition.
qs.x: The data show a clear dose‑dependent inhibition; activity is not independent of concentration. Trap: Option A may seem plausible because the peptide performs best at neutral/alkaline pH, but the statement is true, not false.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best help elucidate the mechanism of action of AP‑42?
o: Determine the peptide’s secondary structure by circular dichroism
Circular dichroism shows the peptide's shape, not what it does to bacteria.
Measure the peptide’s half‑life in serum
Serum half-life is a pharmacokinetic question, not a mechanism question.
Assess the peptide’s effect on bacterial membrane potential
Evaluate the peptide’s toxicity in mammalian cell lines
Toxicity to mammalian cells is about safety, not how the peptide kills bacteria.
qs.x: Measuring changes in membrane potential directly probes whether the peptide disrupts bacterial membranes, a common antibacterial mechanism for amphipathic peptides. Trap: Option A is useful for structural characterization but does not reveal functional mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Social reproduction describes how advantage is transmitted across generations through schooling, networks, and credentials. Tracking, differential parental involvement, and unequal school resources are proposed channels, and interventions that change one channel may leave others intact.
Investigators followed 3,000 students from entry to graduation across schools with different practices (Table 1).

qs.q: Which practice combination worked best?
qs.x: Correct: Opening access and adding support produced both the highest advanced-course participation and the highest graduation rate. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining practice produced lower figures on both measures. Trap: Treating access alone as sufficient.

qs.q: What does the last row add?
qs.x: Correct: Open enrollment without added staffing produced smaller gains, showing that changing a rule without resources limits the effect. Why the others are wrong: Open enrollment still beat tracking, and staffing clearly mattered. Trap: Reading a weaker result as a failed policy.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Because schools selected their own practices, school characteristics may explain the differences rather than the practices themselves. Why the others are wrong: The remaining features are appropriate. Trap: Reading a multi-school comparison as a randomized trial.

qs.q: Which channel does tracking represent?
qs.x: Correct: Tracking is a school practice that sorts students into different curricula, which is an institutional channel. Why the others are wrong: Involvement, networks, and credentials were not measured here. Trap: Naming a channel the study did not examine.

qs.q: Which added measure would test durability?
qs.x: Correct: Following students after graduation shows whether the gains persist into later education or work. Why the others are wrong: Grades, course counts, and teacher ratings are measured during school. Trap: Confusing more detail with longer follow-up.

h: Share of low-income students in advanced courses

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Migration is described by push factors that drive people from an origin and pull factors that attract them to a destination. Internal migration occurs within a country, while immigration and emigration cross borders, and chain migration follows established networks.
A survey of 1,800 recent movers recorded stated reasons and destination choice (Table 1).

qs.q: Which reason is a push factor?
qs.x: Correct: Losing employment at the origin pushes people to leave. Why the others are wrong: Wages, reunification, and ties operate at the destination. Trap: Classifying any economic reason as a push factor.

qs.q: Which row best illustrates chain migration?
qs.x: Correct: Almost all movers citing reunification went to places where family already lived, which is the network-following pattern chain migration describes. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining row shows a lower share with existing ties. Trap: Choosing the most commonly cited reason instead of the most network-dependent one.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Asking for the single most important reason hides the way push and pull factors typically operate together. Why the others are wrong: Sample size, self-report, and category count are appropriate here. Trap: Treating a forced single answer as a complete account of motive.

qs.q: What is emigration?
qs.x: Correct: Emigration is departure from one's country of origin. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options describe entry, internal movement, and return. Trap: Reversing immigration and emigration.

qs.q: Which added measure would test the network account?
qs.x: Correct: If prior contact with people at the destination predicts the move, the network pathway gains support. Why the others are wrong: Distance, age, and recency do not index network ties. Trap: Using geographic proximity as a proxy for social ties.

h: Share moving to a place with existing family ties

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Impression management is the regulation of information about the self to shape how others perceive us. Goffman distinguished front-stage behavior, performed for an audience, from back-stage behavior, where the performance is relaxed.
Participants completed a self-description task believing it would be seen by a potential employer, a close friend, or no one, and the content was coded (Table 1).

qs.q: Which comparison shows front-stage behavior?
qs.x: Correct: Self-promotion rose sharply when an evaluating audience was expected, which is the front-stage performance Goffman described. Why the others are wrong: The friend comparison shows a small shift, and the remaining pairs hold audience type constant or vary two factors. Trap: Reading any audience effect as front-stage performance.

qs.q: What does the anonymity row show?
qs.x: Correct: Removing identifiability cut self-promotion nearly in half, indicating the behavior depends on being evaluated as an identified person. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim conflicts with the table. Trap: Treating an audience label as the active variable rather than accountability.

qs.q: Which added measure would test Goffman's back-stage claim?
qs.x: Correct: Back-stage behavior is defined by the absence of an audience, so unobtrusive observation when participants believe no one is watching tests the claim. Why the others are wrong: Extra audiences, longer tasks, and typing speed do not create a back-stage condition. Trap: Adding another audience when the claim concerns having none.

qs.q: Which row shows the most modesty?
qs.x: Correct: Modest statements were most common when writing for a close friend. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining row is lower. Trap: Assuming the no-audience row must be the most modest.

qs.q: Which term names managing a spoiled identity?
o: That assigns a role to another.
qs.x: Correct: Stigma management refers to controlling information about a devalued attribute. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms describe performance, role demands, and casting others. Trap: Using front-stage behavior as a synonym for all impression management.

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Fertility is measured by the crude birth rate and by the total fertility rate, the average number of children per woman. Replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 in low-mortality settings, and fertility typically falls as female education and labor force participation rise.
Researchers compared regions on fertility and related measures (Table 1).

qs.q: Which region is nearest replacement level?
qs.x: Correct: A total fertility rate of 2.2 is closest to the replacement figure of about 2.1. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining region is further from replacement. Trap: Choosing the lowest rate rather than the one nearest replacement.

qs.q: What pattern do the three columns show?
qs.x: Correct: Total fertility declines monotonically as female schooling and paid work both increase. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim contradicts the table. Trap: Assigning the pattern to one correlate when both move together.

qs.q: Why can this comparison not separate the two correlates?
qs.x: Correct: Because schooling and paid work rise together across these regions, their separate contributions cannot be estimated. Why the others are wrong: Sample size, measurement, and replacement level are not the obstacle. Trap: Blaming sample size for a collinearity problem.

qs.q: What does the total fertility rate measure?
qs.x: Correct: The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options define other measures. Trap: Confusing the total fertility rate with the crude birth rate.

qs.q: What would below-replacement fertility imply long term?
qs.x: Correct: Sustained fertility below replacement shrinks successive cohorts unless net migration compensates. Why the others are wrong: Decline is delayed by age structure, the child share falls, and the structure does change. Trap: Expecting immediate decline when momentum is present.

h: Share of women in paid work

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is the sum of the enthalpy changes of any set of steps that lead from the same reactants to the same products, because enthalpy is a state function. Standard enthalpies of formation allow ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants).
Students used a calorimeter and published values (Table 1). All values are in kJ/mol.

qs.q: What is the calculated ΔH° for complete combustion of one mole of glucose?
qs.x: Correct: Products give 6(−393.5) + 6(−285.8) = −4,076 kJ; subtracting the reactant's −1,273 kJ gives −2,803 kJ, close to the measured −2,800 kJ. Why the others are wrong: Each omits a term or reverses the sign. Trap: Forgetting the coefficients of 6.

qs.q: Why is ΔH°f of O₂ zero?
o: Its formation is thermally neutral by coincidence
It is a definition, not a coincidence.
It is an element in its standard state
Oxygen does not participate in reactions
Enthalpy is measured relative to a reference.
qs.x: Correct: Standard enthalpies of formation are defined as zero for elements in their most stable form at standard conditions, which provides the reference point. Why the others are wrong: Enthalpy is relative; O₂ reacts; the value is definitional. Trap: Treating the zero as a physical measurement.

qs.q: Why is enthalpy called a state function?
o: It changes with the path taken
That describes work and heat separately.
It can be measured only in a calorimeter
Correct: the path does not matter.
It applies only to combustion reactions
qs.x: Correct: Because ΔH depends only on the states, any convenient sequence of steps gives the same total, which is the basis of Hess's law. Why the others are wrong: Path dependence applies to heat and work individually; ΔH can be calculated; it is general. Trap: Confusing enthalpy with heat along a specific path.

qs.q: Why does the measured value differ slightly from the calculated one?
o: Hess's law fails for large molecules
Enthalpy is not conserved in combustion
qs.x: Correct: A 3-kJ difference out of 2,800 kJ is within experimental uncertainty from incomplete combustion, heat escaping the calorimeter and sample impurities. Why the others are wrong: Hess's law holds; energy is conserved; the tabulated values are measurements. Trap: Treating a small discrepancy as a failure of theory.

qs.q: Why can glucose combustion be calculated by Hess's law even though cells oxidize glucose in many steps?
o: The overall change is path independent
Cells release a different total energy
The total enthalpy change is the same.
It also gives CO₂ and water.
Enzymes change the enthalpy of reaction
qs.x: Correct: Cellular respiration starts and ends with the same species, so the total enthalpy change matches combustion even though the energy is captured in ATP rather than released as heat. Why the others are wrong: The total is the same; catalysts do not change ΔH; the products match. Trap: Confusing how energy is released with how much is released.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: Cognitive dissonance theory holds that holding inconsistent cognitions produces discomfort that people reduce by changing an attitude, changing a behavior, or adding a justification. Dissonance is strongest when the inconsistent act feels freely chosen and publicly committed.

Undergraduates performed an hour of tedious peg turning, then were paid either $1 or $20 to tell a waiting participant the task was enjoyable. A third group completed the task with no request. All then rated how enjoyable the task had been (Table 1).

qs.q: Why did the $1 group rate the task most favorably?
o: A small payment is an insult that is reframed
The theory does not predict insult effects.
A small payment makes the task seem valuable
The payment was for the statement, not the task.
A small payment reduces attention to the task
A small payment poorly justifies the lie
qs.x: Correct: With only $1, the external incentive is too weak to explain having praised a boring task, so the remaining dissonance is reduced by shifting the attitude toward genuine enjoyment. Why the others are wrong: The design manipulated justification, not insult, task value, or attention. Trap: Assuming larger rewards always produce larger attitude change.

qs.q: What does the last row add to the interpretation?
o: Payment size drives all the effects
Payment was held at $1 in that row.
qs.x: Correct: When participants were told the statement was required, perceived free choice was removed and the attitude shift disappeared, identifying choice as a necessary condition. Why the others are wrong: Payment was constant across those two rows, the statement remained public, and the control rating was not in question. Trap: Treating the incentive as the only active variable.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine dissonance as the explanation?
o: Ratings were taken after the statement
That ordering is required by the design.
The control group rated the task negatively
That confirms the task was dull.
The $20 group agreed slightly more often
Compliance rates are not the outcome.
qs.x: Correct: Dissonance theory requires an aversive arousal state that mediates attitude change, so equal discomfort across conditions would remove the proposed mechanism. Why the others are wrong: Compliance rates, measurement order, and the control rating are all consistent with the account. Trap: Mistaking compliance for attitude change.

qs.q: Which cognition pair is dissonant for the $1 group?
o: The task was dull; I praised it
I praised the task; another waited
The task was dull; I was paid $1
I praised the task; I was paid $1
qs.x: Correct: Dissonance arises between the private belief that the task was tedious and the public behavior of praising it. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining pair can be held without contradiction. Trap: Labeling any two cognitions dissonant because they occur together.

qs.q: Adding a justification would most likely involve which thought?
o: That is a future behavior change.
The task was more fun than I admitted
I should not have agreed to speak
qs.x: Correct: Adding consonant cognitions, such as believing the statement served a worthwhile purpose, reduces dissonance without revising either original cognition. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options describe attitude change, added discomfort, and behavior change. Trap: Confusing adding cognitions with changing them.

h: Share who agreed to make the statement
r: Paid $1, told the statement was required

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel neuroprotective agent on neuronal survival after ischemic injury in a rodent model. Eighty rats were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group receiving vehicle, a low‑dose group (10 mg/kg), a medium‑dose group (30 mg/kg), and a high‑dose group (50 mg/kg). After 24 hours of induced ischemia, neuronal survival was quantified by counting surviving neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region. Results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and compared using one‑way ANOVA with post‑hoc Tukey tests. The study found a dose‑dependent increase in neuronal survival, with the high‑dose group showing a statistically significant improvement (p < 0.01) over the control. The authors concluded that the neuroprotective agent could be a promising therapeutic candidate for ischemic stroke. The data table below summarizes the key findings for each treatment group.

qs.q: Which treatment group exhibited the highest mean neuronal survival after ischemic injury?
qs.x: The high‑dose group (50 mg/kg) reported the greatest mean neuronal survival (68.3 ± 5.9 neurons/section), surpassing all other groups. Trap: Choosing the control or a lower dose; the highest mean neuronal survival is the high-dose group's 68.3 neurons/section.

qs.q: Which feature of the experimental design described in the passage most directly reduces the chance that pre‑existing differences between rats explain the differences in neuronal survival?
o: Random assignment of rats to treatment groups
Counting surviving neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region
Analyzing the data with one‑way ANOVA and post‑hoc Tukey tests
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment spreads pre-existing differences among rats evenly across groups by chance, so they are unlikely to account for group differences. Why the others are wrong: B) Counting neurons in CA1 defines the outcome measure and does nothing about group composition. C) ANOVA with Tukey tests is a statistical analysis applied after the data are collected and does not alter who is in which group. D) Several doses allow a dose-response to be seen but do not balance rat characteristics across groups. Trap: Selecting the dose-response feature because the passage stresses a dose-dependent effect, although it does not address baseline differences between animals.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute difference in mean neuronal survival between the high‑dose and control groups.
qs.x: Difference = 68.3 - 45.2 = 23.1 neurons/section. Trap: Option B (28.1) is not obtained by any correct operation; adding SDs (5.3 + 5.9 = 11.2) or subtracting the wrong rows also gives wrong values.

qs.q: Which statement is a common misinterpretation of the study’s findings?
o: The low‑dose group’s difference from control did not reach p < 0.05 (p = 0.08).
The high-dose group's improvement over control was statistically significant (p < 0.01).
Mean neuronal survival rose with increasing dose.
The study proves the agent will work in humans.
qs.x: Correct: A rodent study cannot prove efficacy in humans; the statement that it does is the misinterpretation. Why the others are wrong: A) the low-dose p-value in Table 1 is 0.08, above 0.05, so this is accurate. B) the table reports p < 0.01 for the high dose, so this is accurate. C) mean survival rose from 45.2 to 52.1, 58.7 and 68.3 neurons/section with dose, so this is accurate. Trap: Treating a significant result in rats as proof of efficacy in humans.

qs.q: How do these findings contribute to the broader understanding of neuroprotection after ischemic injury?
o: They demonstrate that any drug can protect neurons.
They support dose‑dependent neuroprotection by targeted agents.
They prove that ischemic injury is reversible.
They show that vehicle controls are unnecessary.
qs.x: The study provides evidence that increasing doses of a specific agent enhance neuronal survival, aligning with the concept that targeted neuroprotective strategies can mitigate ischemic damage. Trap: Option A overstates the generalizability of the results.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of the inhibitor X on the activity of enzyme Y. The enzyme activity was quantified by measuring the absorbance at 340 nm, which correlates with product formation. Five concentrations of inhibitor X (0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 µM) were tested in triplicate. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The data show a clear dose‑dependent decrease in absorbance, suggesting inhibition of enzyme Y. The researchers noted that at concentrations above 20 µM, the absorbance values plateaued, indicating possible saturation of the inhibitory effect. The study aims to determine the IC50 value of inhibitor X and to evaluate whether the inhibition follows a competitive or non‑competitive mechanism.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which concentration of inhibitor X results in the greatest reduction in enzyme activity compared to the control?
o: 5 µM reduced activity less than the higher concentrations did.
20 µM reduced activity by 44%, just short of 40 µM's 45.6%.
qs.x: Absorbance at 40 uM (0.68) is the lowest, a reduction of (1.25-0.68)/1.25 = 45.6% versus 44.0% at 20 uM. The effect is nearly plateaued but 40 uM is still marginally greatest. Trap: Choosing 20 uM because inhibition plateaus there; the 40 uM value is still slightly lower.

qs.q: Which control would best show that inhibitor X itself does not change the 340 nm reading independent of the enzyme?
o: Inhibitor X at each concentration in assay buffer with no enzyme
Enzyme and substrate with no inhibitor (0 µM)
Enzyme without substrate at 40 µM inhibitor
qs.x: Correct: Inhibitor X in buffer with no enzyme reveals any absorbance or reaction contributed by X alone. Why the others are wrong: B) this is the 0 µM control already in the table and contains no inhibitor. C) a buffer‑only blank contains no inhibitor, so it cannot reveal an effect of X. D) without substrate no product forms, so this does not isolate the inhibitor's effect on the reading. Trap: Option C tempts readers to treat a buffer blank as a control for the inhibitor.

qs.q: Calculate the percent inhibition of enzyme Y at 10 µM inhibitor X relative to the control.
o: 30% comes from treating the 0.30 drop as a percentage without dividing by 1.25.
50% would need absorbance to fall to about 0.63.
qs.x: Percent inhibition = (1.25 - 0.95)/1.25 x 100 = 0.30/1.25 x 100 = 24%. Trap: Reporting 30% (the raw absorbance difference x100) without dividing by the control value of 1.25.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: Absorbance fell as inhibitor concentration rose from 0 to 20 µM.
Absorbance at 40 µM was only 0.02 lower than at 20 µM.
Enzyme activity was completely abolished at 40 µM.
Absorbance at 10 µM was lower than at 5 µM.
qs.x: Correct: Absorbance at 40 µM was still 0.68, versus 1.25 for the control, so substantial activity remained. Why the others are wrong: A) values were 1.25, 1.10, 0.95 and 0.70. B) 0.70 minus 0.68 is 0.02. D) 0.95 is lower than 1.10. Trap: Option C tempts readers to equate a plateau with zero activity.

qs.q: Which broader pharmacological concept does this study exemplify?
o: The study measured enzyme activity, not how strongly a drug binds a receptor.
Absorption is about how a drug enters the body, which wasn't measured.
Clearance is about how a drug is removed, which wasn't measured.
qs.x: The study demonstrates a classic dose–response curve, where increasing inhibitor concentration leads to progressively greater inhibition of enzyme activity. Trap: Students may confuse binding affinity (A) with the observed dose–response relationship.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers investigated the impact of a novel probiotic strain, L. fermentum X, on the gut microbiome composition and fecal pH levels in a controlled mouse model. Twenty-four male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to three groups: Control (no probiotic), Placebo (vehicle only), and Treatment (daily oral gavage of 1×10⁹ CFU L. fermentum X). Over a 4‑week period, fecal samples were collected weekly and analyzed for pH and microbial diversity via 16S rRNA sequencing. The probiotic group exhibited a statistically significant reduction in fecal pH (6.5 versus 7.2 in the Control group), alongside an increase in beneficial Bacteroidetes relative abundance. No adverse effects were observed. The study suggests that L. fermentum X may modulate gut acidity and microbial balance, potentially influencing host metabolic pathways.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the change in mean fecal pH observed in the Treatment group compared to the Control group?
o: The mean fecal pH increased by 0.7 units.
pH fell from 7.2 to 6.5, so it didn't increase.
The mean fecal pH decreased by 0.7 units.
The mean fecal pH decreased by 0.5 units.
The mean fecal pH remained unchanged.
The mean changed by 0.7 units, so it wasn't unchanged.
qs.x: Mean pH fell from 7.2 to 6.5, a 0.7‑unit decrease. Trap: Option A misleads by stating an increase rather than a decrease.

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates the effect of L. fermentum X itself from the effect of the gavage vehicle?
o: Control at week 1 versus Control at week 4
qs.x: Correct: Treatment and Placebo mice both received gavage, so they differ only in the probiotic (6.5 versus 7.1, a 0.6 difference). Why the others are wrong: A) Control mice received no gavage, so this comparison mixes probiotic and vehicle effects. C) this comparison shows only the vehicle effect (0.1 unit). D) this compares the same untreated group over time and says nothing about the probiotic. Trap: Comparing Treatment with the untreated Control, which confounds the probiotic with the vehicle and gavage procedure.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean fecal pH from Control to Treatment?
o: 12.5% would be a drop of 0.9 units.
15.8% is too large for a 0.7 drop from 7.2.
20% would be a drop of about 1.4 units.
qs.x: Percent reduction = (7.2 − 6.5)/7.2 × 100 ≈ 9.7 %. Trap: Using the wrong baseline for percent change; the 0.7 pH drop must be divided by the Control mean (7.2), not the Treatment mean.

qs.q: Which conclusion is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: L. fermentum X lowers fecal pH in mice.
The data support this: treated mice had lower fecal pH.
The probiotic group had a higher mean pH than the Control group.
The vehicle alone had a minor effect on pH.
The data support this: the vehicle had only a small effect.
No adverse effects were observed in the Treatment group.
The passage supports this: no adverse effects were seen.
qs.x: The Treatment group’s mean pH (6.5) is lower than the Control group’s (7.2), so option B is false. All other statements are supported by the data. Trap: Option A is tempting because it states the correct effect, but the question asks for the unsupported conclusion.

qs.q: Which broader physiological concept is most directly linked to the observed decrease in fecal pH?
o: Insulin resistance isn't directly tied to gut pH.
Renal acid-base balance concerns blood pH, not the gut lumen.
Brain neurotransmission doesn't explain a drop in fecal pH.
qs.x: Lower fecal pH often reflects increased SCFA production by gut microbes, which acidify the lumen. SCFAs are linked to metabolic health, making option B the most relevant link. Trap: Option A might attract students due to the metabolic focus, but insulin resistance is not directly measured here.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes central-route processing, in which argument quality drives persuasion under high motivation and ability, from peripheral-route processing, in which cues such as source attractiveness or message length drive persuasion under low motivation or ability.

Adults read a message supporting a new campus policy. Personal relevance was manipulated by saying the policy would start next year or in ten years. Argument quality and source expertise were varied independently (Table 1).

qs.q: Which pattern indicates central-route processing?
o: Source expertise mattered under low relevance
Argument quality mattered under high relevance
Expert sources produced change under high relevance
Attitude change was positive in every cell
qs.x: Correct: Under high relevance, strong arguments produced far more change than weak ones regardless of source, which is the signature of effortful argument scrutiny. Why the others are wrong: The expertise effect under low relevance is peripheral, overall direction says nothing about route, and the expert cells differ mainly by quality. Trap: Reading any large effect as central processing.

qs.q: Which cell pair isolates the peripheral cue?
o: High relevance expert versus low relevance expert
Low relevance strong versus high relevance weak
qs.x: Correct: Holding relevance low and argument quality constant while varying source expertise isolates the effect of a peripheral cue. Why the others are wrong: The remaining comparisons vary quality, relevance, or both. Trap: Comparing cells that differ on more than one factor.

qs.q: Why is peripheral persuasion typically less durable?
o: It depends on source memory alone
qs.x: Correct: Attitudes formed without elaboration lack supporting argument structure, so they are less resistant to counterargument and decay faster. Why the others are wrong: Immediate magnitude, repetition, and source recall do not define durability. Trap: Equating a large initial shift with a lasting one.

qs.q: Which added condition would best test ability rather than motivation?
o: Tell participants the policy starts sooner
Offer a reward for reading carefully
qs.x: Correct: A distraction limits the cognitive capacity available for elaboration while leaving motivation intact, which separates ability from motivation. Why the others are wrong: Timing and rewards manipulate motivation, and length functions as a cue. Trap: Treating all manipulations of elaboration as equivalent.

qs.q: What does the low-relevance, non-expert cell show?
qs.x: Correct: Without motivation or a credible cue, neither message produced meaningful change. Why the others are wrong: The quality gap was negligible, change was positive, and no expert cue was present. Trap: Reading a trivial difference as an effect.

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (US) comes to elicit a conditioned response. Taste aversion learning is unusual: a single pairing works, and the delay between tasting and illness can be hours. This selectivity (preparedness) reflects the adaptive value of associating flavors, rather than sights or sounds, with sickness.
Rats drank flavored water and then received one of several treatments. Later, consumption of the flavored water was measured (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does nausea produce aversion to flavor but shock does not?
o: They avoided the light paired with shock.
Nausea is more painful than shock
Pain intensity is not the explanation.
Shock is not an unconditioned stimulus
It is a strong US for other associations.
qs.x: Correct: Animals readily link tastes with internal illness and external cues with external pain, a selectivity that reflects evolved predispositions. Why the others are wrong: Shock conditions other cues well; rats detect shock; intensity is not the factor. Trap: Ranking stimuli by strength instead of by biological fit.

qs.q: Why is the 6-hour delay result notable for conditioning theory?
o: Most conditioning needs a short delay
Delay has no effect on any learning
qs.x: Correct: In typical classical conditioning, intervals longer than seconds to minutes produce weak learning, yet taste aversion forms across hours, which fits the slow onset of real food poisoning. Why the others are wrong: Delays weaken most conditioning; learning occurred; the delay did matter. Trap: Generalizing one exception to all conditioning.

qs.q: In this experiment, what is the unconditioned stimulus?
o: It is part of the apparatus.
Correct: it causes nausea without learning.
qs.x: Correct: Lithium chloride produces nausea naturally, so it is the US; the flavor becomes the conditioned stimulus. Why the others are wrong: The flavor is the CS, avoidance is the CR, and the bottle is context. Trap: Mislabeling the CS as the US.

qs.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops nausea at the sight of the clinic. Which process explains this?
qs.x: Correct: The clinic becomes a conditioned stimulus through pairing with the nausea-inducing drug, producing anticipatory nausea before treatment. Why the others are wrong: No reinforcement of a voluntary response occurs; direct experience explains it; habituation reduces responses. Trap: Choosing operant conditioning for any learned clinical response.

qs.q: Why does the light-shock result support the preparedness idea?
o: Correct: matching cue types learn best.
Shock produces no learning at all
qs.x: Correct: Rats learned to avoid the light paired with shock while ignoring the flavor, which shows that cue-outcome pairings follow biologically sensible lines. Why the others are wrong: The light was conditioned; shock produced learning; preference is irrelevant. Trap: Concluding a stimulus cannot be conditioned at all.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: The foot-in-the-door technique obtains compliance with a large request by first securing agreement to a small one, which shifts self-perception toward being a helpful person. The door-in-the-face technique works in reverse, using reciprocal concession after an extreme request is refused.

Canvassers approached 600 households about placing a large yard sign supporting road safety. Some were first asked to sign a petition, others to accept an extreme request, and others were asked directly (Table 1).

qs.q: Which result best supports a self-perception account?
o: Removal times were shortest in the direct group
qs.x: Correct: Longer retention after the small request suggests participants came to see themselves as supporters rather than merely yielding to pressure in the moment. Why the others are wrong: The extreme-request effect reflects concession, and the direct group is a baseline with few placements. Trap: Treating compliance rates alone as evidence about mechanism.

qs.q: What does the last row suggest?
o: That row used no extreme request.
qs.x: Correct: Compliance fell sharply when a different canvasser made the second request, indicating the effect depends partly on continuity of the interaction. Why the others are wrong: The petition still outperformed baseline, no concession was involved, and retention remained long. Trap: Concluding a technique failed when it merely weakened.

qs.q: Which design flaw most threatens these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Without random assignment, pre-existing differences between households could produce the compliance differences independently of technique. Why the others are wrong: Recording, single-site sampling, and constant message content are not internal-validity threats here. Trap: Confusing limited generalization with confounding.

qs.q: Which request sequence defines door-in-the-face?
o: Extreme request, then a smaller one
Small request, then a larger one
qs.x: Correct: Door-in-the-face begins with an extreme request that is expected to be refused, so the smaller follow-up appears as a concession. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining sequence describes the other technique or a control. Trap: Reversing the two sequences.

qs.q: Which measure would best distinguish the two mechanisms?
o: Number of signs on nearby lawns
Total time spent with the canvasser
qs.x: Correct: Self-perception predicts a shift in self-image, whereas reciprocal concession does not, so measuring self-image separates the accounts. Why the others are wrong: Duration, neighborhood signs, and income do not distinguish the mechanisms. Trap: Choosing a measure that both accounts predict equally.

h: Share agreeing to the large sign
Mean days before the sign was removed
r: Extreme request first, then the sign

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: In operant conditioning, reinforcement schedules affect response rate and persistence. Continuous reinforcement rewards every response. Fixed-ratio schedules reward after a set number of responses and produce bursts with brief post-reinforcement pauses; variable-ratio schedules reward after an unpredictable number and produce high steady rates that resist extinction. Fixed-interval schedules produce scalloped patterns.
Pigeons were trained on different schedules, then reinforcement was discontinued (Table 1).

qs.q: Why is the variable-ratio group most resistant to extinction?
o: It received the most total reinforcements
It was trained for the longest time
Correct: the animal cannot tell when reward stopped.
qs.x: Correct: Because reinforcement already came after unpredictable numbers of responses, a long run without reward resembles normal training, so responding continues far longer. Why the others are wrong: Reinforcement rate, effort and training were matched. Trap: Attributing persistence to the amount of reward.

qs.q: Why does the fixed-interval schedule give a lower response rate?
o: Pigeons cannot track time at all
Only one response after the interval is needed.
qs.x: Correct: Only the first response after the interval elapses is reinforced, so rapid early responding gains nothing and animals pause then accelerate near the end. Why the others are wrong: Reinforcement occurs; pigeons track intervals; fewer responses are required. Trap: Confusing interval and ratio requirements.

qs.q: Which schedule describes a slot machine?
o: Payouts would come on a clock.
Correct: payouts come after unpredictable numbers of plays.
qs.x: Correct: Slot machines pay after an unpredictable number of plays, which produces high steady play and strong persistence. Why the others are wrong: Each would make payouts predictable in count or time. Trap: Confusing variable ratio with variable interval.

qs.q: A parent sometimes gives in to a child's tantrums. Why does this make tantrums persistent?
qs.x: Correct: Occasional success creates a variable-ratio pattern, which is the most resistant to extinction, so the behavior continues through many unrewarded episodes. Why the others are wrong: Reinforcement is intermittent, not continuous; giving in rewards; extinction is possible. Trap: Thinking inconsistent reward weakens a behavior.

qs.q: Why does continuous reinforcement extinguish fastest?
o: Correct: every response used to pay.
It produces the highest response rate
It involves no learning at all
qs.x: Correct: When every response has been rewarded, the first few unrewarded responses are a clear signal that conditions have changed, so responding stops quickly. Why the others are wrong: Its rate was the lowest; learning occurred; it uses the most rewards. Trap: Assuming more reward always means stronger behavior.

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: Observational learning occurs when behavior is acquired by watching a model, without direct reinforcement of the observer. Bandura's work identified four necessary processes: attention, retention, reproduction and motivation. Vicarious reinforcement, in which the model is seen to be rewarded, raises the chance that the observer performs the behavior.
Children watched a video of an adult acting aggressively toward a toy, with different endings, then played alone (Table 1). Aggressive acts were counted over 10 minutes.

qs.q: Why do children who saw the model rewarded act most aggressively?
o: They could not remember the video
They were themselves rewarded with candy
Aggression is unlearned in all children
qs.x: Correct: Seeing the model rewarded increases the observer's expectation that the behavior pays, which raises performance even though the child was never reinforced. Why the others are wrong: Children got no reward; memory was required; the control group differed. Trap: Confusing vicarious with direct reinforcement.

qs.q: Why do children who saw the model scolded still act somewhat aggressively?
o: Their rate matched the control group
They did not watch the video
qs.x: Correct: Observers acquire the behavior regardless of the model's outcome; consequences mainly affect whether they choose to perform it, so a small amount of imitation remains. Why the others are wrong: They watched; scolding discourages; their rate exceeded control. Trap: Equating no performance with no learning.

qs.q: Which process is required for a child to copy a complex action?
o: Observational learning does not require it.
Behavior is not inherited this way.
qs.x: Correct: Bandura identified attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; without retaining a representation, the behavior cannot be reproduced later. Why the others are wrong: Direct reinforcement is not required; classical conditioning and inheritance are different processes. Trap: Assuming all learning requires reinforcement of the learner.

qs.q: Why does this design include a group with no video?
o: It tests whether children can see
It proves that videos cause aggression
Causal claims need the comparison itself.
It increases the number of conditions only
It shows the baseline rate of aggression
qs.x: Correct: Without a no-video baseline of 1.9 acts, there would be no way to judge how much each video ending raised aggression. Why the others are wrong: Vision is not tested; the group serves a purpose; the claim rests on the comparison. Trap: Dismissing a control as a formality.

qs.q: Why might these findings not generalize to everyday media exposure?
o: A brief lab session differs from daily life
Children in the study were not real participants
Observational learning does not occur outside labs
qs.x: Correct: Short exposure, an unfamiliar setting, a specific toy and immediate opportunity to imitate differ from the varied and socially regulated conditions of daily media use. Why the others are wrong: Participants and measurements were real; observational learning is general. Trap: Rejecting the mechanism rather than questioning generalization.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Nonverbal communication includes facial expression, gaze, posture, gesture, and paralanguage. Some facial expressions of basic emotion show high cross-cultural recognition, while gestures and display rules vary widely by culture.
Participants from four regions identified photographed expressions and culture-specific gestures (Table 1).

qs.q: Which stimulus type shows the strongest cultural specificity?
qs.x: Correct: Gesture recognition fell by 57 points across regions, far more than any other stimulus, which marks it as culturally learned. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining type shows a modest decline. Trap: Assuming all nonverbal channels are equally universal.

qs.q: What does the facial expression row support?
qs.x: Correct: High but not perfect cross-regional accuracy supports a universal core modified by cultural factors. Why the others are wrong: The remaining claims overstate or contradict the row. Trap: Reading high accuracy as evidence of complete universality.

qs.q: Which concept explains why expressions are suppressed in some settings?
o: Correct: cultural norms for showing emotion.
qs.x: Correct: Display rules are culturally learned norms governing when and how strongly emotions may be shown. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms name a theory, vocal features, and spatial behavior. Trap: Explaining suppression by the absence of the emotion.

qs.q: What is paralanguage?
qs.x: Correct: Paralanguage covers nonverbal vocal features such as tone, pitch, and rate. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options name verbal content, gesture, and posture. Trap: Including word choice in paralanguage.

qs.q: Which design feature strengthens these comparisons?
qs.x: Correct: Presenting the same photographs and clips to every region ensures that differences reflect the viewers rather than the stimuli. Why the others are wrong: Region count, outcome choice, and age range do not control stimulus differences. Trap: Mistaking sample breadth for stimulus control.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Attraction is shaped by proximity, which increases mere exposure and the chance of interaction, and by similarity, reciprocity, and physical attractiveness. The mere exposure effect describes increased liking for repeatedly encountered stimuli.
Residents of a new apartment building were surveyed about friendships after one year, with assignment to units made by lottery (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the lottery strengthen this study?
o: The survey came after a year
qs.x: Correct: Random allocation of units means residents did not choose neighbors they already liked, so proximity can be treated as an assigned variable. Why the others are wrong: Survey timing, group count, and self-report do not address selection. Trap: Treating a long follow-up as a substitute for assignment.

qs.q: Which mechanism do the encounter data support?
qs.x: Correct: Friendship rates rose with reported encounters, which is the pathway the mere exposure account predicts. Why the others are wrong: None of the remaining factors were measured in this study. Trap: Invoking a mechanism the design did not assess.

qs.q: Which finding would most complicate the proximity account?
qs.x: Correct: If friendship rates were unrelated to encounter frequency, proximity could not be acting through exposure and interaction. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining result is consistent with the account. Trap: Treating a predicted result as a complication.

qs.q: Which comparison isolates floor separation?
qs.x: Correct: Comparing residents four doors apart on one floor with residents on different floors sharing a stairwell holds walking distance roughly constant while varying floor. Why the others are wrong: The remaining comparisons vary two factors or hold floor constant. Trap: Comparing the extreme rows.

qs.q: What is the mere exposure effect?
qs.x: Correct: Repeated encounters with a neutral stimulus tend to increase liking for it. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options name other determinants of attraction. Trap: Merging exposure with similarity.

h: Share naming the other as a friend

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Health insurance affects access through coverage breadth, cost sharing, and network adequacy. Underinsurance describes having coverage that still leaves high out-of-pocket costs, and coverage alone does not guarantee timely care.
A survey of 5,000 adults recorded coverage type and care experiences (Table 1).

qs.q: Which group best illustrates underinsurance?
qs.x: Correct: Adults with high-deductible plans had coverage but still faced substantial out-of-pocket burden and frequent cost-related delay, which is the definition of underinsurance. Why the others are wrong: The uninsured are not insured at all, and the remaining groups show lower cost burden. Trap: Equating any access problem with underinsurance.

qs.q: Which barrier does the narrow network row highlight?
qs.x: Correct: With low cost burden but elevated delay, the limiting factor is the availability of participating providers. Why the others are wrong: Cost burden was low, coverage was present, and literacy was not measured. Trap: Attributing every access problem to cost.

qs.q: Which inference is unwarranted?
qs.x: Correct: People select or are sorted into coverage types by income, employment, and health, so a causal claim is not supported. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining statement is descriptive. Trap: Treating coverage categories as an assigned treatment.

qs.q: Which group least often had a usual source of care?
qs.x: Correct: Uninsured adults least often reported a usual source of care. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining group was higher. Trap: Reading the delay column.

qs.q: Which policy would the table most support?
qs.x: Correct: Because covered adults with high deductibles still delayed care, reducing cost sharing addresses the gap the table documents. Why the others are wrong: Coverage counts alone miss underinsurance, narrower networks worsen access, and data publication does not change costs. Trap: Measuring success by coverage rates alone.

h: Share delaying care due to cost
Mean out-of-pocket spending as a share of income
Share with a usual source of care

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: Glucose in solution cyclizes when the C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 aldehyde, forming a six-membered pyranose ring with a new stereocenter at C1 (the anomeric carbon). β-D-glucopyranose has the C1 OH equatorial; α-D-glucopyranose has it axial. The two anomers interconvert through the open-chain form, a process called anomerization, and reducing sugars have a free anomeric carbon that can be oxidized.
Students dissolved pure α-D-glucose in water and followed the optical rotation over time (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the rotation change over time?
o: The ring opens permanently to the straight chain
The open form is a minor intermediate.
Correct: the mixture reaches a fixed ratio.
qs.x: Correct: α-D-glucose opens to the aldehyde and recloses as either anomer until the equilibrium mixture of about 36% α and 64% β is reached, which has a rotation of +52.7°. Why the others are wrong: Glucose does not decompose; water is not an oxidant; the open chain is less than 1% at equilibrium. Trap: Thinking the sugar changes identity.

qs.q: Why is the β anomer favored at equilibrium?
o: It is a different sugar entirely
It cannot convert back to the α form
qs.x: Correct: In the chair conformation, an equatorial substituent at C1 avoids steric interactions, so the β anomer is slightly lower in energy and more abundant. Why the others are wrong: Both have the same groups; they are the same sugar; interconversion is reversible. Trap: Explaining the ratio by composition rather than conformation.

qs.q: Which carbon of glucose is the anomeric carbon in the pyranose ring?
o: Correct: it becomes a hemiacetal carbon.
C5 contributes the ring oxygen's carbon.
C6 stays outside the ring as CH₂OH.
C3, in the middle of the chain
qs.x: Correct: The aldehyde carbon C1 becomes the hemiacetal (anomeric) carbon when C5's hydroxyl attacks it. Why the others are wrong: C5's OH supplies the ring oxygen; C6 remains exocyclic; C3 is unchanged. Trap: Confusing the attacking hydroxyl's carbon with the anomeric carbon.

qs.q: Why is glucose a reducing sugar but sucrose is not?
o: Sucrose contains no carbonyl or anomeric carbons at all
qs.x: Correct: A reducing sugar needs a free anomeric carbon that can open to an aldehyde. In sucrose, glucose and fructose are joined through both anomeric carbons, so neither ring can open. Why the others are wrong: Its anomeric carbons exist but are blocked; glucose has a hemiacetal; size is irrelevant. Trap: Assuming all disaccharides are nonreducing.

qs.q: Why does the rotation stop changing after about 4 hours?
o: Correct: the ratio no longer changes.
qs.x: Correct: Once the forward and reverse anomerization rates are equal, the composition and therefore the observed rotation are constant. Why the others are wrong: Glucose remains in solution; the instrument reads a value; no crystallization occurs. Trap: Reading a constant value as the end of the reaction rather than equilibrium.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: Esters hydrolyze to a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Base-catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) is effectively irreversible because the carboxylate product is deprotonated. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is reversible. Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is an ester that hydrolyzes to salicylic acid and acetic acid, which is why old aspirin tablets smell of vinegar.
Students measured the rate of aspirin hydrolysis at 37 °C in buffers of different pH (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does hydrolysis speed up at high pH?
o: Protons catalyze faster at high pH
Proton concentration is low at high pH.
Correct: a stronger nucleophile is present.
The ester becomes nonpolar at high pH
Polarity is not the key factor.
qs.x: Correct: Hydroxide is a far better nucleophile than water, so it attacks the ester carbonyl directly and the rate rises steeply with pH. Why the others are wrong: Protons are scarce at high pH; polarity is not the issue; the ionized form is more soluble. Trap: Assuming acid catalysis dominates at every pH.

qs.q: Why does lowering the temperature slow hydrolysis so much?
o: Fewer collisions exceed the activation energy
Correct: rate constants fall with temperature.
The pH changes to 2 at low temperature
Aspirin becomes a different compound when cold
qs.x: Correct: The Arrhenius relation means the fraction of collisions with enough energy falls sharply as temperature drops, so the rate constant falls from 0.085 to 0.011 h⁻¹. Why the others are wrong: Water is liquid; pH is buffered; aspirin is unchanged. Trap: Looking for a phase or chemical change rather than kinetics.

qs.q: How many hours are needed for 75% of aspirin to hydrolyze at pH 7.4 and 37 °C?
o: This is half of one half-life.
qs.x: Correct: After one half-life 50% remains, and after two half-lives 25% remains, so 75% has hydrolyzed in about 16.4 hours. Why the others are wrong: Each uses the wrong number of half-lives. Trap: Confusing the fraction remaining with the fraction reacted.

qs.q: What are the products of aspirin hydrolysis?
o: The acyl group is acetyl, not ethyl.
qs.x: Correct: Cleaving the ester bond gives the phenol-containing salicylic acid and acetic acid, whose smell gives old tablets a vinegar odor. Why the others are wrong: No ethanol or sugar is formed; hydrolysis changes the molecule. Trap: Confusing the alcohol and acid portions of the ester.

qs.q: Why should aspirin tablets be stored in a cool, dry place?
o: Light converts aspirin into salicylic acid
Hydrolysis, not light, is the issue here.
Cold air removes the acetyl group
Water and heat both speed hydrolysis
qs.x: Correct: Hydrolysis requires water and accelerates with temperature, so keeping tablets dry and cool preserves the active ester. Why the others are wrong: The mechanism is hydrolysis; cold slows it; dryness slows it. Trap: Reversing the role of moisture.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: A centrifuge spins samples in a circle of radius r at angular speed ω. Particles experience a centripetal acceleration a = ω²r directed toward the axis. Relative centrifugal force (RCF, or "g-force") is this acceleration divided by g. Sedimentation rate rises with RCF, so larger accelerations separate smaller particles.
A laboratory rotor has a radius of 0.10 m at the tube bottom. Samples were spun at different speeds and the time for a marker protein to pellet was recorded (Table 1). Note 1 rpm = 2π/60 rad/s.

qs.q: Why does RCF rise fourfold when speed doubles?
o: RCF depends on the radius squared
Then doubling would only double it.
qs.x: Correct: a = ω²r, so doubling the angular speed multiplies the acceleration by four, as seen from 1,006 to 4,023 × g. Why the others are wrong: Radius is fixed; the dependence is quadratic; acceleration does not depend on mass. Trap: Assuming a linear relation.

qs.q: What is the centripetal acceleration at 6,000 rpm?
o: This drops a factor of ten.
qs.x: Correct: a = ω²r = (628)² × 0.10 ≈ 394,000 × 0.10 ≈ 39,400 m/s², which is about 4,000 × g. Why the others are wrong: Each omits the square or a factor. Trap: Forgetting to square the angular speed.

qs.q: In which direction does the net force on a sedimenting particle point?
o: Correct: centripetal force keeps it on its circular path.
Gravity is small compared with the centrifugal effect.
Away from the axis, pushing the particle out
There is no outward real force.
qs.x: Correct: Circular motion requires a net inward (centripetal) force; particles pellet outward because the liquid cannot supply enough inward force for the denser particles. Why the others are wrong: The "centrifugal force" is not a real force in an inertial frame; the net force is inward. Trap: Treating the outward sensation as a force.

qs.q: Why does pelleting time fall as RCF rises?
o: Higher speeds lower the liquid's viscosity to zero
The tube becomes shorter at high speed
Particles become denser at high speed
qs.x: Correct: Sedimentation velocity is proportional to the applied acceleration, so a 16-fold higher RCF pellets the protein in about one-sixteenth of the time. Why the others are wrong: Viscosity, geometry and density do not change. Trap: Looking for a change in the particles rather than in the field.

qs.q: Two proteins have the same mass but different shapes. Which will sediment faster?
o: Both sediment at exactly the same rate
The more compact one, with less drag
Correct: shape affects the friction coefficient.
The more elongated one, since it is longer
qs.x: Correct: Sedimentation depends on mass, buoyancy and the frictional drag coefficient, which is smaller for compact shapes, so the compact protein moves faster. Why the others are wrong: Elongated shapes have higher drag; shape matters; salt is not required. Trap: Considering mass alone.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Kowalski laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 50-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
o: 0.124 is the change per minute, not over 2 minutes.
0.299 is the 2-minute reading itself; you still need to subtract the 0.05 starting value.
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.299 − 0.05 = 0.249. Trap: Subtracting the 0 min reading from the 3 min reading (0.423 - 0.05 = 0.373) instead of the 2 min reading.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To ensure the enzyme is saturated
A blank without substrate can't show whether the enzyme is saturated.
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
The extinction coefficient is a fixed property of NADH; a blank can't change it.
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
A blank doesn't convert anything; it measures background change.
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Believing the blank saturates the enzyme or raises the signal, when its purpose is to reveal non-enzymatic absorbance change.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 20 µM/min in the cuvette; 20 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
This forgets to multiply by the 50-fold dilution for the homogenate.
0.02 µM/min in the cuvette; 1 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.02 µM/min misplaces the decimal; ΔA per min ÷ 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ gives about 20 µM/min.
1000 µM/min in the cuvette; 50000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1000 µM/min in the cuvette multiplies by 50 one time too many.
20 µM/min in the cuvette; 1000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1244/6220 = 20 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 50-fold dilution to get 1000 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting the 50-fold dilution and reporting the cuvette rate of 20 µM/min as the activity of the undiluted homogenate.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
This is true: only NADH absorbs at 340 nm.
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vₘₐₓ
This is true: saturating substrate makes the rate approach Vₘₐₓ.
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
This is true: the early linear part reflects the initial velocity.
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing NAD⁺ also absorbs strongly at 340 nm so the signal tracks total coenzyme; only NADH absorbs there, which makes the assay work.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A radioactive ATP assay tracks phosphate transfer, not NADH at 340 nm.
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size; it doesn't measure activity over time.
Coupling PK's pyruvate to LDH and NADH use
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
An immunoassay measures how much enzyme is present, not its activity.
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a radioactive, gel or antibody assay, none of which links enzyme activity to NADH absorbance at 340 nm.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: Tendons store elastic energy. For small stretches a tendon behaves like a spring, with force F = kx and stored energy U = ½kx². In running, the Achilles tendon stretches during landing and recoils during push-off, returning much of the stored energy and lowering the metabolic cost of running.
Researchers measured force and elongation in cadaver Achilles tendons (Table 1), then estimated energy return during a running stride.

qs.q: How much energy is stored in tendon 1 at peak load?
o: This drops a factor of ten.
This omits the factor of ½.
This multiplies force by elongation in millimeters.
qs.x: Correct: U = ½kx² = ½ × 180,000 N/m × (0.010 m)² = 9.0 J. Why the others are wrong: Each omits the ½ or mishandles units. Trap: Using millimeters instead of meters.

qs.q: Why does tendon elasticity lower the cost of running?
o: It removes the need for muscle contraction
It prevents the foot from touching the ground
Stored energy is returned at push-off
It converts heat into mechanical work
Heat is not recovered this way.
qs.x: Correct: Energy stored while the tendon stretches during landing is released during recoil, so muscles supply less of the work needed for each stride. Why the others are wrong: The foot lands; heat is not converted back; muscles still contract. Trap: Treating elastic storage as a replacement for muscle work.

qs.q: Which tendon is stiffest, and what does that mean?
o: Tendon 1, which has the largest peak force
Tendon 2, which stretches least per newton
qs.x: Correct: Stiffness is force per unit elongation; tendon 2 has the highest k, so it elongates least for a given force. Why the others are wrong: More stretch means less stiff; peak force alone is not stiffness. Trap: Equating strength with stiffness.

qs.q: What is the unit of the spring constant k?
o: That is force expressed differently but not the standard form here.
This is a rate of force change.
qs.x: Correct: k has units of N/m, since F = kx. Why the others are wrong: N·m is energy or torque; N/s is a rate. Trap: Confusing the units of stiffness and energy.

qs.q: Why does the energy returned by a real tendon fall short of ½kx²?
o: The tendon gains mass during loading
Correct: tendons are not perfectly elastic.
qs.x: Correct: Real tendons show hysteresis: the unloading curve lies below the loading curve, and the difference appears as heat, so about 90–93% of stored energy is returned. Why the others are wrong: Energy is conserved; mass is constant; forces were measured. Trap: Assuming biological springs are ideal.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Hemophilia A results from loss-of-function variants in F8, a gene on the X chromosome that encodes clotting factor VIII. A genetics clinic traced a three-generation family after a 6-year-old boy (III-2) presented with prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction. His factor VIII activity was 3% of normal.

The boy's mother (II-2) and maternal grandfather (I-1) were tested. The grandfather, who had a lifelong history of joint bleeds, carried the same F8 variant. The mother's factor VIII activity was 58% of normal and she was heterozygous. The boy's father (II-3) and his sister (III-1) were also tested. Table 1 summarizes the results.
Clinicians noted that some heterozygous women have factor VIII levels below 40% and mild bleeding, a finding attributed to skewed X-chromosome inactivation in the cells that produce factor VIII.

qs.q: Which pattern of inheritance best fits this family?
