o: Autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance in females only
The variant is on the X chromosome and heterozygous females are usually unaffected.
X-linked recessive, via a carrier daughter
Correct: affected males are linked through an unaffected carrier female.
Y-linked, passed directly from father to son in each generation
The proband's father does not carry the variant.
Mitochondrial, passed from the grandfather to all of his grandchildren
Mitochondrial traits pass through mothers, and fathers do not transmit them.
qs.x: Correct: An affected male (I-1) passed his X to his daughter, who is a heterozygous carrier, and she passed it to her son. Skipping through a carrier female is the hallmark of X-linked recessive inheritance. Why the others are wrong: Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation and both sexes equally; mitochondrial traits come only from mothers; Y-linked traits pass father to son, but this father is normal. Trap: Assuming that because two males are affected, the trait must pass father to son.

qs.q: If II-2 has another son with a man who does not carry the variant, what is the probability that the son will have hemophilia A?
o: The mother is a carrier, so sons are at risk.
Correct: the son receives one of his mother's two X chromosomes.
This is the chance that any child, not a son, is an affected boy.
This multiplies probabilities that are not independent here.
qs.x: Correct: A son gets his X only from his mother, who has one variant X and one normal X, so the risk is 1/2. Why the others are wrong: 1/4 answers a different question (an affected son among all children). 1/8 has no basis in this cross. 0 ignores that the mother is a carrier. Trap: Answering for 'any child' when the question already specifies a son.

qs.q: Why can III-1 be heterozygous yet have lower factor VIII activity than her mother?
o: Heterozygous females always express only the paternal X chromosome
Inactivation is random, not always paternal.
She inherited two copies of the variant from both of her parents
Her father carries a normal F8 allele.
Factor VIII is encoded on an autosome as well as on the X chromosome
F8 is only on the X chromosome.
Her cells may inactivate the normal X more often than the variant X
Correct: skewed inactivation can leave mostly the variant X active.
qs.x: Correct: In each female cell one X is silenced at random early in development. If, by chance, most factor VIII-producing cells silence the normal X, activity falls (here to 35%). Why the others are wrong: Her father is normal, F8 is X-linked only, and inactivation is random rather than fixed to one parent. Trap: Expecting every heterozygote to have the same level of expression.

qs.q: Which statement about the proband's father (II-3) is supported by the data?
o: He must be a silent carrier because his son is affected
Males have one X; a carrier male would be affected, and his level is normal.
His normal factor level shows the variant is recessive in males
Males are hemizygous, so dominance does not apply to them.
He could not have passed it on; sons get his Y
Correct: fathers give sons a Y chromosome, not an X.
He transmitted the variant to his daughter III-1
His F8 genotype is normal, so her variant came from her mother.
qs.x: Correct: A father contributes his Y to sons and his X to daughters, so the boy's variant X came from his mother. Why the others are wrong: Males cannot be silent carriers of an X-linked trait; the father is normal, so III-1's variant came from II-2; dominance is not tested in hemizygous males. Trap: Assuming an affected child must have an affected or carrier father.

qs.q: Factor VIII activity in the family was measured at a single clinic visit. What is the main limitation of using this one value to classify carriers?
o: Levels vary with stress and pregnancy
Correct: factor VIII is an acute-phase protein whose level fluctuates.
Activity assays cannot detect factor VIII in women
The assay works the same in both sexes.
One measurement makes the pedigree autosomal
The inheritance pattern does not depend on how often levels are measured.
Genotype was not measured, so carrier status is unknown
Genotype was measured, as Table 1 shows.
qs.x: Correct: Factor VIII rises with stress, inflammation, pregnancy and in people with non-O blood types, so a single level can overlap between carriers and non-carriers. That is why genotyping is the definitive test. Why the others are wrong: The assay works in women; measurement timing does not change the pattern of inheritance; and genotypes were in fact reported. Trap: Treating a single biochemical value as equivalent to a genotype.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: Differential centrifugation separates cell components by size and density. A tissue homogenate is spun at increasing speeds; each pellet is collected before the supernatant is spun again faster. Marker enzymes identify which organelles are in each fraction.
Rat liver was homogenized in isotonic sucrose and spun in four steps. Activities of four marker enzymes were measured in each pellet, expressed as percent of the total activity recovered (Table 1).

qs.q: Which fraction is richest in mitochondria?
o: Correct: succinate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial marker.
This contains microsomes from the ER.
qs.x: Correct: Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II) is in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and 84% of its activity is in P2. Why the others are wrong: P1 holds nuclei (DNA polymerase); P3 holds ER fragments (glucose-6-phosphatase); the supernatant holds soluble cytosolic enzymes such as lactate dehydrogenase. Trap: Assuming the biggest pellet holds the most important organelle.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use isotonic sucrose?
o: To supply energy to the mitochondria
Sucrose is not used by mitochondria.
To keep organelles from swelling or bursting
Correct: isotonic solution prevents osmotic damage.
To make all organelles the same density so they pellet together
Density differences are needed for separation.
The enzymes must stay active to be measured.
qs.x: Correct: Isotonic sucrose matches organelle osmolarity, so membranes stay intact and enzymes stay where they belong. Why the others are wrong: Mitochondria cannot use sucrose; equal density would prevent separation; denatured enzymes could not be assayed. Trap: Thinking sucrose is added as a nutrient.

qs.q: Which fraction would contain the most ribosome-studded membrane fragments?
o: Nuclei and unbroken cells pellet here.
Correct: rough ER forms microsomes that pellet at high speed.
qs.x: Correct: Homogenization breaks the ER into small vesicles called microsomes, which pellet only at about 100,000 g and carry glucose-6-phosphatase. Why the others are wrong: Lower speeds pellet larger organelles; microsomes are removed before the final supernatant. Trap: Confusing free ribosomes with rough ER fragments.

qs.q: Some succinate dehydrogenase appears in P1. What is the best explanation?
o: The enzyme is secreted from cells
The 1,000 g spin breaks open the mitochondria in the sample
Breaking them would release enzymes to lighter fractions.
Some mitochondria pellet with whole cells
qs.x: Correct: Differential centrifugation gives enriched, not pure, fractions; unbroken cells and clumped organelles carry some mitochondria into P1. Why the others are wrong: Nuclei lack this enzyme; it is not secreted; broken mitochondria would move to lighter fractions. Trap: Expecting perfect separation.

qs.q: Which enzyme's distribution shows that most cells were broken open?
o: Correct: a cytosolic enzyme was released.
DNA polymerase, found mostly in the P1 pellet
This shows where nuclei went, not cell breakage.
qs.x: Correct: Lactate dehydrogenase is a soluble cytosolic enzyme; 91% in the supernatant shows that most cells released their cytosol. Unbroken cells would carry it into P1. Why the others are wrong: These markers show organelle locations, not cell lysis. Trap: Choosing a marker that tracks organelles rather than cytosol.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: Triacylglycerols are esters of glycerol and three fatty acids. Saponification with sodium hydroxide cleaves them to glycerol and three fatty acid salts (soaps), which are amphipathic: a nonpolar tail and an ionized carboxylate head. Above a critical concentration, soap molecules form micelles with tails inward, which solubilize grease.
Students saponified 100 g of a fat and analyzed the products (Table 1). The average molar mass of the fat was 860 g/mol.

qs.q: Why are three moles of NaOH needed per mole of fat?
o: NaOH acts as a catalyst only
Soap molecules each need three sodium ions
Each of three ester bonds is cleaved
qs.x: Correct: A triacylglycerol has three ester linkages, and base-mediated hydrolysis consumes one hydroxide per ester, giving a 1:3 ratio that matches 0.110 and 0.330 mol. Why the others are wrong: Glycerol is a product; NaOH is a reactant; each soap carries one sodium. Trap: Treating the base as a catalyst.

qs.q: Why does soap remove grease from skin?
o: Micelles trap oil in nonpolar cores
Soap chemically digests fats into glucose
Grease dissolves in water once warmed
qs.x: Correct: Soap tails dissolve in the grease while the charged heads face water, so oil is suspended as micelles and rinses away. Why the others are wrong: Soap does not digest fats; water stays polar; grease alone is insoluble. Trap: Assuming the cleaning action is chemical breakdown.

qs.q: What percentage yield of glycerol was obtained from 100 g of fat?
o: This uses the mass of glycerol directly.
Correct: 0.110 mol obtained of 0.116 mol possible.
Yield cannot exceed the theoretical amount.
qs.x: Correct: 100 g ÷ 860 g/mol = 0.116 mol of fat, which could give 0.116 mol of glycerol; 0.110 ÷ 0.116 ≈ 95%. Why the others are wrong: Mass percentage is not yield; the soap value is a different species. Trap: Comparing masses instead of moles.

qs.q: Why is a soap molecule described as amphipathic?
o: It has polar and nonpolar regions
Correct: an ionic head and a hydrocarbon tail.
It can act as an acid or a base
It dissolves in neither water nor oil
qs.x: Correct: The long hydrocarbon chain is nonpolar and the carboxylate head is charged, so the molecule interacts with both water and oil. Why the others are wrong: Amphoteric describes acid-base behavior; soap interacts with both phases; one head group is present. Trap: Confusing amphipathic with amphoteric.

qs.q: Why do soaps form scum in hard water?
o: Hard water has too few ions
Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form insoluble salts
Hard water protonates all soap heads
Hard water is not strongly acidic.
qs.x: Correct: Divalent cations bind two carboxylate heads each, forming insoluble calcium and magnesium salts that precipitate as scum, which is why detergents with sulfonate heads are preferred. Why the others are wrong: Hard water is not acidic; soap is not volatile; hard water is ion rich. Trap: Thinking hardness acts through pH.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: Microtubules are hollow polymers of α/β-tubulin dimers that grow and shrink by dynamic instability. They form the mitotic spindle, serve as tracks for kinesin and dynein motors, and form the core of cilia and flagella. Colchicine binds free tubulin dimers and prevents their addition to microtubules, while taxol binds polymerized microtubules and stabilizes them.

Researchers treated cultured fibroblasts for 4 hours with colchicine, taxol, or cytochalasin D (which blocks actin polymerization). They measured the percentage of cells arrested in metaphase, the speed of labeled vesicles moving along the cell, and cell migration into a scratch wound (Table 1).

qs.q: Why do both colchicine and taxol arrest cells in metaphase despite opposite actions on tubulin?
o: Both depolymerize the actin ring needed for cytokinesis
Both block the dynamics the spindle needs
Correct: spindles require growth and shrinkage.
Both bind to centromeres and block attachment
Both drugs prevent DNA replication in S phase
Arrest occurs in metaphase, after replication.
qs.x: Correct: Chromosome capture and alignment depend on microtubules that grow and shrink. Preventing growth (colchicine) or shrinkage (taxol) both block normal spindle function, activating the spindle checkpoint. Why the others are wrong: Arrest occurs after S phase; actin is not their target; they bind tubulin. Trap: Expecting drugs with opposite actions to have opposite effects.

qs.q: Which conclusion about vesicle transport is best supported?
o: It is driven by diffusion through the cytosol
Diffusion would not depend on microtubules.
It requires cells to be in metaphase to occur at all
It depends mainly on actin filaments
Correct: both tubulin drugs slow it.
qs.x: Correct: Colchicine and taxol each lower transport speed about tenfold, while blocking actin has little effect, so long-range vesicle transport uses microtubule tracks with motor proteins. Why the others are wrong: Cytochalasin barely changes speed; diffusion is not microtubule-dependent; transport occurs throughout interphase. Trap: Ignoring the actin control.

qs.q: Which motor protein carries vesicles toward the plus end of microtubules?
o: Dynein moves toward the minus end.
Correct: most kinesins move toward the plus end.
This is the subunit of the track, not a motor.
qs.x: Correct: Kinesins generally walk toward microtubule plus ends, which lie at the cell periphery, carrying cargo outward. Why the others are wrong: Dynein moves toward minus ends; myosin uses actin; tubulin is structural. Trap: Mixing up the directions of kinesin and dynein.

qs.q: Which treatment most strongly impairs wound closure, and why?
o: None, because migration is unaffected by the cytoskeleton
Cytochalasin D, since migration needs actin
Colchicine, because migration needs the spindle
Taxol, because it destroys all actin filaments in the cell
qs.x: Correct: Cytochalasin D lowers wound closure to 8%, the smallest value, because cells extend lamellipodia by polymerizing actin at their leading edge. Microtubule drugs also slow migration, partly by blocking cell polarity and division. Why the others are wrong: Spindles are not used for crawling; taxol targets microtubules; every drug reduced closure. Trap: Choosing a microtubule drug because it caused the most metaphase arrest.

qs.q: Colchicine is used for gout. Based on the passage, which cellular process would it most likely impair in neutrophils?
o: Colchicine does not target DNA synthesis.
Colchicine does not inhibit glycolytic enzymes.
qs.x: Correct: Neutrophil movement and degranulation require microtubules, so colchicine reduces their migration into joints and the inflammation that follows. Why the others are wrong: DNA synthesis is not targeted; neutrophils are not antibody producers; glycolysis is not affected. Trap: Choosing a process from a different cell type.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood Ca²⁺ by stimulating bone resorption, increasing renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, reducing renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulating the kidney to make calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which increases intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption. Low Ca²⁺ is detected by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells.
An endocrine service reviewed four patients with abnormal Ca²⁺ (Table 1). Reference ranges: Ca²⁺ 8.5–10.2 mg/dL, PTH 15–65 pg/mL, phosphate 2.5–4.5 mg/dL.

qs.q: Why is phosphate low in Patient A?
o: PTH stimulates phosphate absorption in the gut
Calcitriol raises gut phosphate absorption, not lower it.
High Ca²⁺ blocks phosphate release from bone
qs.x: Correct: PTH inhibits proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption, so excess PTH causes phosphate loss in urine. Why the others are wrong: Gut absorption would raise phosphate; adenomas do not store phosphate; bone resorption releases phosphate. Trap: Expecting Ca²⁺ and phosphate to move in the same direction.

qs.q: What explains high PTH with low Ca²⁺ in Patient B?
o: This raises Ca²⁺ and lowers PTH.
A parathyroid adenoma secretes excess PTH
An adenoma would cause high Ca²⁺.
qs.x: Correct: In kidney disease, phosphate builds up and calcitriol falls, so Ca²⁺ drops and the parathyroids respond by secreting more PTH. Why the others are wrong: Adenomas cause hypercalcemia; removal lowers PTH; PTHrP suppresses PTH. Trap: Calling any high PTH an adenoma.

qs.q: Why is PTH low in Patient C?
o: The lung tumor has spread to and destroyed the parathyroids
There is no evidence of destruction.
qs.x: Correct: PTH-related peptide acts on PTH receptors and raises Ca²⁺; the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptors detect the high Ca²⁺ and stop PTH secretion. Why the others are wrong: Glands are not destroyed; standard assays do not detect PTHrP as PTH; kidney failure raises PTH. Trap: Expecting PTH to rise whenever Ca²⁺ is high.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of Patient D's findings?
qs.x: Correct: Low PTH with low Ca²⁺ and high phosphate after neck surgery suggests the parathyroid glands were removed or damaged. Why the others are wrong: Vitamin D excess raises Ca²⁺; secondary hyperparathyroidism raises PTH; PTHrP raises Ca²⁺. Trap: Missing the clue in the notes column.

qs.q: Which treatment would best correct Patient D's Ca²⁺ in the long term?
o: Correct: bypasses the missing PTH step.
A drug that blocks the calcium-sensing receptor
Few parathyroid cells are left to respond.
Removal of the remaining parathyroid tissue
qs.x: Correct: Without PTH, the kidney makes little calcitriol, so oral Ca²⁺ is poorly absorbed. Giving active vitamin D with Ca²⁺ restores intestinal uptake. Why the others are wrong: Calcium alone is poorly absorbed; receptor drugs need functional glands; removing tissue worsens the problem. Trap: Overlooking PTH's role in activating vitamin D.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: In Drosophila melanogaster, the recessive alleles b (black body), pr (purple eyes) and vg (vestigial wings) lie on chromosome 2. A student crossed females heterozygous at all three loci (b pr vg / b⁺ pr⁺ vg⁺, all wild-type alleles on one homolog) with males homozygous recessive at all three (b pr vg / b pr vg). Male Drosophila do not undergo crossing over, but this does not affect a testcross because the male contributes only recessive alleles.

The 2,000 progeny were classified by phenotype (Table 1). Map distances were calculated as the percentage of recombinant offspring between each pair of genes, counting double crossovers in both intervals.

qs.q: Which two classes are the double-crossover progeny?
o: Correct: they are the two least frequent classes.
These arise from a single crossover between b and pr.
Wild type and black, purple, vestigial
These are the most frequent parental classes.
These arise from a single crossover between pr and vg.
qs.x: Correct: Double crossovers require two independent exchange events and are therefore the rarest classes (16 + 16). Why the others are wrong: The most common classes are parental; the remaining pairs are single-crossover products. Trap: Picking the rarest single class rather than the rarest reciprocal pair.

qs.q: Comparing the parental and double-crossover classes, which gene is in the middle?
o: vg, because vestigial is the most common phenotype
Phenotype frequency does not identify the middle gene.
b, because black appears in the most classes
Frequency of a trait does not identify gene order.
The order cannot be found without a reciprocal cross
A three-point testcross alone gives the order.
pr, the only allele that switches
Correct: double crossovers swap the middle gene relative to the outer two.
qs.x: Correct: Parental b pr vg becomes double-crossover b pr⁺ vg: only pr changes, so pr lies between b and vg. Why the others are wrong: Gene order comes from comparing parental and double-crossover classes, not from how common a phenotype is, and no reciprocal cross is needed. Trap: Assuming genes are in the order they are named.

qs.q: What is the map distance between b and pr?
o: This counts the pr–vg recombinants instead.
This is the full b–vg distance.
qs.x: Correct: Recombinants between b and pr are the single crossovers in that interval (120) plus the double crossovers (32): 152 / 2,000 = 7.6%. Why the others are wrong: 6.0 leaves out double crossovers; 23.0 is the pr–vg interval; 30.6 is the b–vg total. Trap: Forgetting that each double crossover is also a crossover in each interval.

qs.q: The expected frequency of double crossovers, if the two intervals were independent, is 0.076 × 0.23 ≈ 0.0175. What does the observed frequency of 0.016 suggest?
o: Strong positive interference that prevents all double crossovers
Double crossovers did occur at near the expected rate.
The genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently
Recombination frequencies well under 50% show linkage.
Correct: coefficient of coincidence ≈ 0.91, so interference ≈ 0.09.
Crossing over happened in males as well as females
Males contribute only recessive alleles here.
qs.x: Correct: Coincidence = observed / expected = 0.016 / 0.0175 ≈ 0.91, and interference = 1 − 0.91 ≈ 0.09, a small effect. Why the others are wrong: Complete interference would give zero double crossovers; frequencies below 50% mean linkage; and male crossing over is irrelevant in this testcross. Trap: Reading any shortfall of double crossovers as complete interference.

qs.q: Why was a testcross to a triple-recessive male used rather than a cross between two heterozygotes?
o: It makes crossing over happen more often in the heterozygous female
The tester does not change the female's recombination rate.
Offspring phenotypes reveal the female's alleles
Correct: the tester adds only recessive alleles.
It ensures all offspring are female and easier to score
It removes the need to count large numbers of offspring
Large counts are still needed for accurate frequencies.
qs.x: Correct: Because the male contributes b pr vg, every recessive phenotype reflects the female's gamete, so recombinant gametes can be counted directly. Why the others are wrong: The tester does not alter recombination, sample size still matters, and both sexes are produced. Trap: Thinking the tester parent influences recombination.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: During fasting, falling glucose lowers insulin and raises glucagon. Glucagon acts on the liver through a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP. In the first day, glycogenolysis supplies most glucose; after that, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids becomes the main source. With prolonged fasting, the liver also makes ketone bodies from fatty acids, and the brain gradually uses them as fuel.
Healthy volunteers fasted for 5 days under medical supervision. Blood samples were collected each morning (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does glucose stay near 65 mg/dL rather than continuing to fall?
o: Muscle releases free glucose from its glycogen
Glycogen stores increase as the fast goes on
Glycogen is depleted in about a day.
Insulin secretion rises to protect the brain
Gluconeogenesis and ketone use spare glucose
Correct: production rises and demand falls.
qs.x: Correct: The liver makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids, while rising ketones let the brain use less glucose, so glucose levels off. Why the others are wrong: Glycogen falls; insulin drops; muscle cannot release free glucose. Trap: Assuming glycogen is the main source throughout a fast.

qs.q: Why do ketone bodies rise steeply by day 3?
o: The brain releases ketone bodies into the blood
qs.x: Correct: Low insulin and high glucagon activate lipolysis; fatty acids reach the liver, where β-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA that is converted into ketone bodies. Why the others are wrong: The brain uses but does not make ketones; ketones come from fat; insulin is low. Trap: Thinking the brain makes its own ketones.

qs.q: Which second messenger mediates glucagon's effects in the liver?
o: This is used by nitric oxide signaling.
Correct: glucagon receptors couple to Gs.
qs.x: Correct: Glucagon activates Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, which activates PKA. Why the others are wrong: cGMP is used by NO; IP₃ is a Gq messenger; IRS belongs to the insulin pathway. Trap: Mixing up the second messengers of different receptors.

qs.q: Why is the brain's use of ketone bodies important for survival during prolonged fasting?
o: It allows the brain to use fatty acids directly
Fatty acids do not cross into the brain well.
It spares protein used for gluconeogenesis
Correct: less muscle is broken down.
qs.x: Correct: Less glucose demand means less gluconeogenesis from amino acids, which preserves muscle protein during a long fast. Why the others are wrong: Fatty acids are not a main brain fuel; insulin remains low; glycogen is not refilled. Trap: Forgetting the protein cost of gluconeogenesis.

qs.q: Which change would be expected in urinary nitrogen between day 1 and day 5?
o: It falls as protein breakdown slows
It rises steadily throughout the fast
It does not change during fasting
qs.x: Correct: Early in a fast, amino acids supply gluconeogenesis and urinary nitrogen is high; as ketones replace glucose in the brain, protein breakdown and nitrogen loss fall. Why the others are wrong: Nitrogen loss falls later; it does not reach zero; it does change. Trap: Assuming catabolism increases steadily the longer one fasts.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Sickle cell disease is caused by homozygosity for the HbS allele of the β-globin gene (HBB). Heterozygotes (HbAS) are largely healthy and are partly protected against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Researchers screened 1,000 randomly selected newborns at a regional hospital in a malaria-endemic area using hemoglobin electrophoresis.

They found 640 HbAA, 330 HbAS and 30 HbSS newborns. The team compared these counts with the counts expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. They also screened 1,000 adults aged 20–40 years from the same region and found 590 HbAA, 404 HbAS and 6 HbSS individuals.

qs.q: What is the frequency of the HbS allele among the newborns?
o: This is the frequency of HbSS genotypes.
This is the frequency of newborns carrying any HbS allele.
qs.x: Correct: Each heterozygote carries one HbS allele and each HbSS newborn carries two: 330 + 60 = 390 alleles out of 2,000, so q = 0.195. Why the others are wrong: 0.165 omits homozygotes; 0.36 is a carrier-or-affected proportion; 0.03 is a genotype frequency. Trap: Confusing genotype frequency with allele frequency.

qs.q: Using q = 0.195, how many HbAS newborns would be expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
o: This is q² × 1,000, the expected HbSS count.
This is pq × 1,000, missing the factor of 2.
This is p² × 1,000, the expected HbAA count.
qs.x: Correct: 2pq = 2 × 0.805 × 0.195 ≈ 0.314, or about 314 newborns, close to the observed 330. Why the others are wrong: 38 and 648 are the other genotype expectations; 157 forgets the factor of two. Trap: Dropping the 2 in 2pq.

qs.q: Compared with newborns, adults have more HbAS and far fewer HbSS individuals. Which explanation best fits?
o: Selection against HbSS and for HbAS
Correct: heterozygote advantage and HbSS mortality shift adult counts.
Nonrandom mating among the adults who were screened
Mating affects offspring genotypes, not survival of the adults themselves.
Genetic drift: random changes in a small adult sample
Samples of 1,000 make large chance shifts unlikely.
New mutations converting HbAA to HbAS during childhood
Somatic changes do not alter inherited HBB genotype.
qs.x: Correct: Genotype frequencies change between birth and adulthood only if survival differs. HbSS children often die young without care, while HbAS children survive malaria better. This is balancing selection maintaining the allele. Why the others are wrong: Drift is unlikely with large samples; mutation does not convert genotypes in a lifetime; and mating patterns affect the next generation, not survival. Trap: Invoking nonrandom mating whenever genotype frequencies depart from expectation.

qs.q: Which feature of the study design limits conclusions about selection?
o: The adults were too young to have reached reproductive age
Adults aged 20–40 are of reproductive age.
Electrophoresis cannot separate hemoglobin A from S
Electrophoresis does separate HbA and HbS.
Different people were screened at birth and in adulthood
Correct: cross-sectional groups may differ for reasons besides survival.
Screening newborns at random introduces selection bias
qs.x: Correct: Comparing two different cross-sectional samples assumes that adults born 20–40 years ago started with the same genotype frequencies as today's newborns, and that migration has not changed the population. A cohort followed from birth would be stronger. Why the others are wrong: Electrophoresis distinguishes HbA and HbS; random selection is a strength; and the adults are of reproductive age. Trap: Treating two snapshots as if they followed the same people.

qs.q: Why are HbAS individuals partly protected from severe falciparum malaria?
o: Heterozygotes produce antibodies against all Plasmodium species
Protection is not due to a special antibody response.
HbS binds the parasite directly and prevents it from entering cells
HbS does not block invasion directly.
HbAS red cells lack the receptors that all parasites need
Plasmodium falciparum can still invade HbAS cells.
Infected HbAS cells sickle and are cleared
Correct: early sickling and clearance limit parasite growth.
qs.x: Correct: Parasite metabolism lowers O₂ inside infected HbAS cells, promoting HbS polymerization and sickling. Sickled infected cells are removed by the spleen, limiting parasite growth. Why the others are wrong: HbS does not block invasion, the cells still have the required receptors, and no special antibody is made. Trap: Confusing sickle trait protection with Duffy-negative protection against P. vivax.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: Static equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque. In analyzing the spine, the erector spinae muscles act at a small angle to the spine and a short distance from the lumbosacral joint, while the weight of the upper body and any held load act at much longer horizontal distances when a person bends forward.
Researchers modeled a 70-kg person lifting a 20-kg box with the trunk bent 60° forward. Distances are horizontal from the lumbosacral joint (Table 1).

qs.q: What muscle force balances the upper body weight alone?
o: This multiplies instead of dividing by the lever arm.
qs.x: Correct: F × 5.0 = 446 N × 25 cm, so F ≈ 2,230 N. Why the others are wrong: 446 N is the weight; 89 N inverts the ratio; the last multiplies wrongly. Trap: Inverting the lever arm ratio.

qs.q: Including the 20-kg box, what total muscle force is needed?
o: This is the box term alone.
This omits the box's lever arm.
qs.x: Correct: The box contributes (196 N × 45 cm) ÷ 5.0 cm ≈ 1,764 N, giving about 3,990 N in total. Why the others are wrong: Each omits a term or a lever arm. Trap: Adding weights instead of torques.

qs.q: Why does bending forward greatly increase the load on back muscles?
o: Horizontal lever arms grow as the trunk tilts
Gravity becomes stronger closer to the ground
Muscles lose half their strength when bent
Strength is not halved by posture.
qs.x: Correct: Torque equals force times horizontal distance from the joint; tilting moves the body's and the load's centers of mass farther from the spine, so muscle force must rise. Why the others are wrong: Weight and gravity do not change; muscle strength is not posture-halved. Trap: Looking for a change in weight rather than geometry.

qs.q: Why is lifting with the knees bent and the load close to the body safer?
o: It increases the muscle lever arm greatly
It removes the need for muscle force
It lowers the weight of the load
It shortens the load's lever arm
Correct: less torque at the spine.
qs.x: Correct: Holding the load near the body reduces its horizontal distance from the lumbosacral joint, which directly reduces the required muscle force and joint compression. Why the others are wrong: The muscle lever arm is fixed by anatomy; force is still needed; weight is constant. Trap: Thinking posture changes the muscle's own lever arm.

qs.q: What does the large muscle force imply about the compressive force on the lumbar disc?
o: It is zero because torques balance
Torque balance does not remove force.
Correct: muscle force and body weight both compress.
It acts upward, pulling the spine apart
It equals the weight of the box
qs.x: Correct: The vertical forces include the muscle force pulling down along the spine plus the upper body and load weights, so disc compression exceeds the muscle force. Why the others are wrong: Compression is much larger than the load; balanced torques do not imply zero force; the disc is compressed. Trap: Confusing zero net torque with zero force.

r: Horizontal distance to upper body center of mass

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Petrov laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 50-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
o: 0.187 is the change per minute, not over 2 minutes.
0.423 is the 2-minute reading itself; you still need to subtract 0.05.
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.423 − 0.05 = 0.373. Trap: Reporting 0.187, the change per minute, or the 2-minute absorbance of 0.423 without subtracting the 0.05 starting value.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: A blank doesn't convert anything; it measures background change.
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
The extinction coefficient is fixed; a blank can't change it.
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
A blank without substrate can't show whether the enzyme is saturated.
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank supplies the NADH or sets saturation, rather than showing the signal drift occurring without the enzyme reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 30 µM/min in the cuvette; 30 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
This forgets to multiply by the 50-fold dilution for the homogenate.
0.03 µM/min in the cuvette; 1.5 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.03 µM/min misplaces the decimal; 0.1866 ÷ 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ is about 30 µM/min.
1500 µM/min in the cuvette; 75000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1500 µM/min in the cuvette multiplies by 50 one time too many.
30 µM/min in the cuvette; 1500 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1866/6220 = 30 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 50-fold dilution to get 1500 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting to multiply by the 50-fold dilution, giving 30 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate, or misplacing the decimal in the unit conversion.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
This is true: only NADH absorbs at 340 nm.
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
This is true: the early linear part reflects the initial velocity.
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vₘₐₓ
This is true: saturating substrate makes the rate approach Vₘₐₓ.
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Choosing the statement that NADH absorbs but NAD⁺ does not, which is true, rather than the false claim that both coenzymes absorb at 340 nm.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A radioactive ATP assay tracks phosphate, not NADH at 340 nm.
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
An immunoassay measures how much enzyme is present, not its activity.
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size; it doesn't measure activity.
Coupling PK's pyruvate to LDH and NADH use
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a radioactive, antibody or gel method, none of which monitors NADH absorbance at 340 nm continuously.

passages.title: Fluids in circulation of blood, gas movement, and gas exchange · passage
text: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid tube, Poiseuille's law gives Q = πΔPr⁴ ÷ (8ηL), where Q is flow, ΔP the pressure difference, r the radius, η the viscosity and L the length. Flow depends on the fourth power of radius, so small changes in vessel radius change flow dramatically.
Students pumped a glycerol solution through rigid tubes at a fixed pressure difference of 8.0 kPa and measured flow (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does halving the radius reduce flow 16-fold?
qs.x: Correct: Q ∝ r⁴, so halving the radius multiplies flow by (0.5)⁴ = 1/16, matching 24 to 1.5 mL/min. Why the others are wrong: Each uses the wrong power of r. Trap: Applying the cross-sectional area relation instead.

qs.q: Why does doubling the tube length halve the flow?
o: Longer tubes raise the pressure difference
Longer tubes have a smaller radius
Flow does not depend on length
Flow is inversely proportional to length
qs.x: Correct: In Poiseuille's law L appears in the denominator, so doubling it halves the flow at constant ΔP. Why the others are wrong: Radius and ΔP were fixed; length clearly matters. Trap: Assuming only radius affects resistance.

qs.q: Which change in a blood vessel would most increase flow at a fixed pressure?
o: A 20% increase in vessel wall thickness
Thickness is not in the equation.
Correct: r⁴ gives about a doubling.
qs.x: Correct: A 1.2-fold radius increase multiplies flow by 1.2⁴ ≈ 2.07, far more than the other 20% changes, which act linearly. Why the others are wrong: Length and viscosity changes act in the first power; wall thickness does not enter. Trap: Treating all 20% changes as equivalent.

qs.q: Why does the body regulate blood flow mainly by changing vessel radius?
o: Small radius changes alter flow greatly
Vessel length changes rapidly with activity
Blood pressure cannot be changed at all
Pressure does change, but less selectively.
Blood viscosity can be changed within seconds
qs.x: Correct: Smooth muscle in arterioles can constrict or dilate quickly, and because flow scales with r⁴, modest changes redirect large amounts of blood. Why the others are wrong: Viscosity and length change little and slowly; pressure changes affect the whole system rather than one organ. Trap: Overlooking why local control needs radius.

qs.q: Blood is not a Newtonian fluid. Which observation would show this?
o: Flow depends on the pressure difference
Flow is faster in wider tubes
Viscosity of liquids falls with temperature.
qs.x: Correct: A Newtonian fluid has a viscosity independent of shear rate; blood's apparent viscosity falls at higher shear rates because red cells align and deform. Why the others are wrong: Pressure and radius effects are general; liquid viscosity falls as temperature rises. Trap: Choosing a property shared by all fluids.

passages.title: Fluids in circulation of blood, gas movement, and gas exchange · passage
text: For an incompressible fluid in steady flow, the continuity equation gives A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so narrowing raises speed. Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, then implies that pressure falls where speed rises, at the same height. A stenosis (narrowed segment) therefore shows a high velocity and a low pressure.
A model artery of internal diameter 8.0 mm carried fluid of density 1,050 kg/m³. A rigid insert produced a stenosis. Pressure and velocity were measured in each segment (Table 1).

qs.q: Why is velocity four times higher in the stenosis?
o: Area falls fourfold when diameter halves
The pump speeds up at the stenosis
Pressure pushes the fluid faster through friction
qs.x: Correct: Halving the diameter quarters the cross-sectional area, and continuity requires velocity to rise by the same factor of four. Why the others are wrong: Velocity varies inversely with area; the pump is unchanged; pressure is lower there. Trap: Using diameter instead of area.

qs.q: Why is pressure lowest in the stenosis?
o: Narrow tubes always have higher pressure
The fluid loses mass in the narrow segment
qs.x: Correct: At constant height, the sum of pressure and kinetic energy per volume is nearly constant, so faster fluid has lower pressure. Why the others are wrong: Mass is conserved; pressure falls in the constriction; height is unchanged. Trap: Expecting a squeeze to raise pressure.

qs.q: Why is downstream pressure (95 mmHg) lower than upstream pressure (98 mmHg)?
o: Bernoulli's equation predicts a permanent drop
Ideal flow would recover pressure fully.
Viscous and turbulent losses dissipate energy
Correct: real flow is not ideal.
The fluid became less dense downstream
qs.x: Correct: Bernoulli's equation alone predicts full pressure recovery once the area returns. The residual 3-mmHg loss reflects viscous dissipation and turbulence in the real system. Why the others are wrong: Ideal flow recovers; density is constant; velocity recovers. Trap: Forgetting that Bernoulli's equation ignores friction.

qs.q: What does the continuity equation express?
o: Conservation of mass in steady flow
Conservation of energy along a streamline
Conservation of momentum at a wall
The relation between pressure and temperature
qs.x: Correct: For an incompressible fluid, the volume passing each cross-section per second is the same, which follows from conservation of mass. Why the others are wrong: Energy conservation is Bernoulli's equation; the others are unrelated. Trap: Mixing up the two fluid equations.

qs.q: In a severe arterial stenosis, why can a bruit (murmur) be heard?
o: The artery wall vibrates from low velocity
Laminar flow is noisy at high pressure
High velocity makes the flow turbulent
Blood becomes a gas in the narrow segment
qs.x: Correct: Above a critical Reynolds number, flow becomes turbulent; the chaotic eddies vibrate the vessel and surrounding tissue, producing an audible bruit. Why the others are wrong: Laminar flow is quiet; velocity is high; blood does not vaporize. Trap: Associating sound with pressure rather than turbulence.

passages.title: Fluids in circulation of blood, gas movement, and gas exchange · passage
text: An object in fluid experiences a buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces (Archimedes' principle). Underwater weighing uses this to find body density: a person weighs less in water by the weight of the displaced water. Because fat is less dense (about 0.90 g/cm³) than lean tissue (about 1.10 g/cm³), body density estimates body fat percentage.
Three participants were weighed in air and submerged in water at 36 °C (density 0.994 g/cm³). Residual lung volume was accounted for (Table 1).

qs.q: What volume of water does participant P displace?
o: This drops a factor of ten.
qs.x: Correct: Buoyant force = 686 − 29 = 657 N. Each liter of this water weighs 0.994 kg × 9.8 ≈ 9.74 N, so the volume is 657 ÷ 9.74 ≈ 67 L. Why the others are wrong: Each misuses a value or a factor. Trap: Using the in-water weight as the buoyant force.

qs.q: Which participant has the highest percentage of body fat?
o: Q, with the lowest body density
R, with the highest body density
All have the same, since all float
P, with the largest weight in air
qs.x: Correct: Fat is less dense than lean tissue, so the participant with the lowest whole-body density (1.047 g/cm³) has the greatest fat fraction. Why the others are wrong: High density means leaner; absolute weight says little; densities differ. Trap: Assuming the heaviest person has the most fat.

qs.q: Why must residual lung volume be measured?
o: Residual volume changes body weight in air
Air in the lungs adds buoyancy
Lungs absorb water during the test
qs.x: Correct: Trapped air is very low in density and increases displacement without adding weight, so ignoring it makes the body appear less dense and fatter than it is. Why the others are wrong: Air lowers density; lungs do not take in water; air adds negligible weight. Trap: Getting the direction of the error backward.

qs.q: What determines whether an object floats?
o: Its surface area in contact with water
Its temperature relative to the fluid
Its density compared with the fluid's
qs.x: Correct: An object floats when its average density is less than the fluid's, so the displaced fluid can weigh as much as the object. Why the others are wrong: Weight and area alone do not decide; temperature matters only via density. Trap: Thinking heavy things always sink.

qs.q: Why would the same person have a different apparent weight in sea water?
o: Sea water is less dense than fresh water
It is denser due to dissolved salts.
Salt makes the body heavier in air
Buoyant force depends only on the object
It depends on the fluid displaced.
qs.x: Correct: Salt raises density to about 1.025 g/cm³, so the same displaced volume weighs more, the buoyant force is larger, and apparent weight is smaller. Why the others are wrong: Sea water is denser; buoyancy depends on fluid density; air weight is unchanged. Trap: Forgetting the fluid's role in Archimedes' principle.

passages.title: Electrochemistry and electrical circuits and their elements · passage
text: A neuron's membrane behaves like a resistor and capacitor in parallel. Injecting a steady current I changes the membrane potential toward a final value ΔV = IR, approaching it along an exponential curve with time constant τ = RC. The length constant describes how far a signal spreads passively: it is longer when membrane resistance is high and axial resistance is low.
Researchers injected current into three axons and recorded the voltage change at the injection site (Table 1).

qs.q: Why do axons 1 and 2 reach the same final voltage at different speeds?
o: Correct: R sets ΔV, RC sets speed.
ΔV is a change, not an absolute value.
qs.x: Correct: ΔV = IR depends only on resistance, which is 50 MΩ in both, while τ = RC is twice as long in axon 2 because its capacitance is doubled. Why the others are wrong: Capacitances differ; current is the same; ΔV is a change. Trap: Assuming capacitance changes the final voltage.

qs.q: What is ΔV for axon 3 with 0.2 nA?
o: This drops a factor of ten.
This multiplies by an extra factor of ten.
qs.x: Correct: ΔV = IR = 0.2 nA × 100 MΩ = 0.020 V = 20 mV. Why the others are wrong: Each uses the wrong resistance or exponent. Trap: Slipping a power of ten when mixing nanoamps and megohms.

qs.q: Why does myelin speed passive signal spread along an axon?
o: It removes the axon's axial resistance entirely
It raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance
Correct: longer length constant, shorter time constant.
It lowers membrane resistance so current leaks faster
It raises capacitance so charge builds up
qs.x: Correct: Wrapping the axon adds layers of membrane in series, which increases resistance and decreases capacitance, so current travels farther and the voltage changes faster. Why the others are wrong: Leak and higher capacitance would slow conduction; axial resistance remains. Trap: Confusing series and parallel effects of adding membrane layers.

qs.q: What does a capacitor do in this circuit?
o: Ion gradients and channels do that.
qs.x: Correct: The lipid bilayer is a thin insulator with conductive solutions on each side, so it stores charge like a capacitor. Why the others are wrong: Resistors dissipate heat; capacitors pass transient current; the resting potential comes from ion gradients. Trap: Treating a capacitor as an open circuit at all times.

qs.q: A disease lowers membrane resistance by opening leak channels. What effect on signal spread is expected?
o: Signals travel farther along the axon
The axon becomes myelinated in response
Myelination is not induced this way.
Signals decay over a shorter distance
The time constant becomes much longer
qs.x: Correct: With more leak, current escapes across the membrane sooner, so the length constant falls and passive signals do not reach as far; τ = RC also falls. Why the others are wrong: Leak reduces spread; τ falls; myelination does not occur in response. Trap: Mixing up the effects on the two constants.

passages.title: Electrochemistry and electrical circuits and their elements · passage
text: In a galvanic cell, the half-reaction with the higher reduction potential occurs at the cathode and the other is reversed at the anode. The cell potential is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, and ΔG° = −nFE°cell with F = 96,485 C/mol. A positive E°cell means a spontaneous reaction.
Students built cells from metal electrodes in 1.0 M solutions of their ions at 25 °C (Table 1).

qs.q: What is E°cell for a Cu/Zn cell?
o: This uses only the copper value.
This subtracts in the wrong direction partially.
qs.x: Correct: Copper has the higher potential, so it is the cathode: E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. Why the others are wrong: Each misassigns the electrodes or omits one. Trap: Forgetting the double negative.

qs.q: Which metal is oxidized in a Cu/Zn cell?
o: Correct: it has the lower reduction potential.
qs.x: Correct: The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs in reverse, so zinc metal is oxidized to Zn²⁺ at the anode. Why the others are wrong: Copper is reduced; oxidation defines the anode; one electrode must oxidize. Trap: Mixing up anode and cathode in a galvanic cell.

qs.q: What is ΔG° for the Cu/Zn cell?
o: The sign shows a spontaneous reaction.
qs.x: Correct: ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2)(96,485 C/mol)(1.10 V) ≈ −212,000 J/mol = −212 kJ/mol. Why the others are wrong: n is 2; the sign must be negative; nF cannot be omitted. Trap: Forgetting that both half-reactions transfer two electrons.

qs.q: Which cell from Table 1 gives the smallest positive potential?
qs.x: Correct: Pairing iron with zinc gives −0.44 − (−0.76) = 0.32 V, the smallest positive cell potential available. Why the others are wrong: Cu/Zn is largest; Cu/H₂ is 0.34 V; H₂/Fe is 0.44 V. Trap: Comparing single half-cell values rather than differences.

qs.q: Why is a zinc coating used to protect steel from rusting?
o: Zinc converts iron into a noble metal
Zinc oxidizes in place of iron
Zinc prevents all water contact forever
Zinc has a higher reduction potential than iron
qs.x: Correct: Zinc's lower reduction potential means it is oxidized preferentially, so even scratched galvanized steel is protected while zinc remains. Why the others are wrong: Coatings are imperfect; zinc's potential is lower; iron is unchanged chemically. Trap: Thinking protection depends only on a physical barrier.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Self-esteem is a global evaluation of one's worth, while self-concept is the broader set of beliefs about the self and self-efficacy is confidence in performing a specific task. Self-esteem is relatively stable but responds to domains a person treats as central to identity.
Researchers surveyed 1,500 adolescents, measuring global self-esteem and satisfaction in four domains, and asked how important each domain was (Table 1).

qs.q: What do these correlations suggest?
qs.x: Correct: Domain satisfaction predicts global self-esteem far more strongly when the adolescent considers that domain important, which is the definition of moderation. Why the others are wrong: Appearance only leads among those who value it, direction is undetermined, and the domains differ. Trap: Reading a moderator effect as a main effect.

qs.q: Which construct is measured by domain satisfaction?
qs.x: Correct: Satisfaction with a specific domain is a component belief within the self-concept. Why the others are wrong: Global esteem was a separate measure, and efficacy and locus of control were not assessed. Trap: Treating every self-measure as self-esteem.

qs.q: Which finding would best support stability of self-esteem?
qs.x: Correct: Stability is demonstrated when individuals keep similar relative scores across time, which is what test-retest correlation measures. Why the others are wrong: Internal consistency, domain spread, and mean level address other properties. Trap: Confusing reliability of items with stability over time.

qs.q: Which domain shows the largest moderation gap?
qs.x: Correct: The athletic correlation falls by 0.40, the largest drop in the table. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining domain shows a smaller change. Trap: Choosing the domain with the highest single correlation.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of this design?
o: Four domains suffice for the question.
qs.x: Correct: Because everything was measured at once, the design cannot establish whether domain satisfaction precedes global self-esteem. Why the others are wrong: Domain count and self-report are appropriate, and age restriction limits generalization rather than validity. Trap: Listing a generalization limit as the central flaw.

h: Correlation with global self-esteem, domain rated important
Correlation with global self-esteem, domain rated unimportant

passages.title: Electrochemistry and electrical circuits and their elements · passage
text: In electrolysis, an external power supply forces a nonspontaneous redox reaction. The charge passed is Q = It, and Faraday's laws relate charge to moles of electrons: moles of e⁻ = It ÷ F, with F = 96,485 C/mol. The mass deposited follows from the stoichiometry of the half-reaction.
Students electroplated copper from CuSO₄ solution onto a cathode at a constant 1.5 A (Table 1). The molar mass of copper is 63.5 g/mol.

qs.q: How many moles of electrons pass in 20 minutes?
qs.x: Correct: moles e⁻ = Q ÷ F = 1,800 ÷ 96,485 ≈ 0.0187 mol. Why the others are wrong: Each applies an extra factor or omits F. Trap: Applying the 2-electron stoichiometry at the wrong step.

qs.q: What mass of copper should 1,800 C deposit?
qs.x: Correct: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles Cu = 0.0187 ÷ 2 ≈ 0.00933, and mass = 0.00933 × 63.5 ≈ 0.59 g, matching the data. Why the others are wrong: Each omits a step or uses the wrong charge. Trap: Forgetting that two electrons deposit one copper atom.

qs.q: Why is electrolysis nonspontaneous?
o: Its cell potential is positive but small
qs.x: Correct: The forced reaction has E°cell < 0 and ΔG° > 0, so electrical work from an external source is required. Why the others are wrong: Positive E° and negative ΔG describe spontaneous reactions; external energy is required. Trap: Mixing up the signs of E° and ΔG.

qs.q: At which electrode is copper deposited?
o: Oxidation does not deposit metal here.
Neither, since copper stays in solution
qs.x: Correct: Reduction always occurs at the cathode, where Cu²⁺ gains two electrons and plates out as metal. Why the others are wrong: Oxidation occurs at the anode; deposition is at one electrode; mass was measured. Trap: Mixing up the electrodes between galvanic and electrolytic cells.

qs.q: To deposit silver (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag) instead, how would the mass per coulomb compare?
o: Exactly the same moles per coulomb
Fewer moles of metal per coulomb
One electron per atom needs less charge.
More moles of metal per coulomb
Correct: only one electron is needed.
qs.x: Correct: Because silver requires one electron per atom instead of two, the same charge deposits twice as many moles of metal. Why the others are wrong: Fewer electrons per atom means more atoms; stoichiometry differs; silver does plate. Trap: Comparing masses without accounting for electron stoichiometry and molar mass separately.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: When cells are placed in a solution, water moves by osmosis toward the side with higher concentration of impermeant solutes. Human red blood cells (RBCs) have an internal osmolarity of about 290 mOsm/L. A solution is isotonic when it causes no net change in cell volume, which depends on whether solutes can cross the membrane.

A student placed RBCs in five solutions and measured cell volume after 10 minutes and the percentage of cells that lysed (Table 1). Urea crosses the RBC membrane readily, while NaCl and sucrose do not.

qs.q: Why did cells lyse in 300 mM urea although its osmolarity is close to 290 mOsm/L?
o: Urea enters, and water follows it
Correct: a permeant solute is not effective osmotically.
Urea is hypertonic, so cells shrink and burst
Urea does not dissolve membranes at this concentration.
Urea pumps Na⁺ into the cells actively
qs.x: Correct: Urea crosses the membrane until its concentration is equal on both sides. Inside, it adds to the cell's own impermeant solutes, so water enters and the cells swell and burst. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic. Why the others are wrong: Urea is not a detergent; shrinking cells crenate; urea does not pump ions. Trap: Equating isosmotic with isotonic.

qs.q: Which solution caused the cells to shrink the most?
qs.x: Correct: 2.0% NaCl is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and volume falls to 0.62. Why the others are wrong: 0.45% NaCl is hypotonic; sucrose and 0.9% NaCl are near isotonic. Trap: Confusing hypotonic and hypertonic.

qs.q: Why did only 45% of cells lyse in 0.45% NaCl?
o: Cells differ in how much swelling they withstand
Half the cells were already isotonic to the solution
All cells began at about 290 mOsm/L.
NaCl at this concentration repairs membranes
Half the cells lack aquaporins and cannot swell
qs.x: Correct: Older and more spherical RBCs have less spare membrane and burst sooner, so lysis in a moderately hypotonic solution is partial. Why the others are wrong: Average volume rose; salt has no repair effect; cells started with the same osmolarity. Trap: Expecting an all-or-none response from a population.

qs.q: Which term describes 300 mM sucrose relative to RBCs?
o: Sucrose does not cross the RBC membrane.
qs.x: Correct: Sucrose cannot cross the membrane and has nearly the same osmolarity as cytoplasm, so volume barely changes. Why the others are wrong: Large volume changes would occur in strongly hypo- or hypertonic solutions; sucrose is impermeant. Trap: Treating every solute as permeant like urea.

qs.q: A patient receives a large volume of 5% dextrose in water (about 280 mOsm/L) intravenously. What happens to RBC volume after the glucose is taken up and metabolized?
o: It decreases, because water moves into the kidney tubules
This does not determine RBC volume.
It decreases, because glucose raises plasma osmolarity
It stays the same, because the solution was isosmotic
Isosmotic is not isotonic once glucose is used.
It increases, because free water is left
Correct: the solution becomes effectively hypotonic.
qs.x: Correct: Glucose is transported into cells and metabolized, leaving water that dilutes plasma and causes cells to swell. Why the others are wrong: Glucose does not stay in plasma; isosmotic does not mean isotonic; renal handling does not set RBC volume directly. Trap: Judging tonicity by initial osmolarity alone.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence built from mastery experience, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, and interpretation of physiological arousal. Mastery experience is generally the strongest source.
Adults enrolled in a swimming course were randomly assigned to one of four confidence-building approaches before their first deep-water attempt (Table 1).

qs.q: Which result fits the theory's ranking of sources?
qs.x: Correct: Graded mastery produced the highest efficacy ratings and completion, matching the prediction that direct success is the most powerful source. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining statement contradicts the table. Trap: Assuming verbal persuasion is strong because it is common.

qs.q: Why is a similar peer used for modeling?
qs.x: Correct: Vicarious experience is most effective when the observer judges the model to be comparable, so success seems attainable. Why the others are wrong: Speed, arousal, and advice are not what similarity supplies. Trap: Treating any model as equally informative.

qs.q: Which design change would best isolate arousal interpretation?
o: Shorten the course by a week
qs.x: Correct: Telling participants that a racing heart signals readiness manipulates the interpretation of arousal while leaving the arousal itself intact. Why the others are wrong: More sessions, additional measurement, and a shorter course do not alter interpretation. Trap: Confusing reducing arousal with reinterpreting it.

qs.q: How does self-efficacy differ from self-esteem?
o: It is a stable personality trait
qs.x: Correct: Self-efficacy refers to confidence in a particular task rather than overall worth. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options describe self-esteem, traits, or contradict the data. Trap: Using the two terms interchangeably.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported?
qs.x: Correct: Completion was highest in the mastery condition, though all approaches produced some completion. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim overstates or misreads the table. Trap: Reading a weaker effect as no effect.

passages.title: Self-identity · passage
text: Erikson described eight psychosocial stages, each posing a conflict whose resolution shapes later development. Adolescence centers on identity versus role confusion, and Marcia extended this into four identity statuses defined by exploration and commitment.
Clinicians interviewed 60 young adults about career and value commitments and classified each by identity status (Table 1).

qs.q: Which status describes commitment without exploration?
qs.x: Correct: Foreclosure involves adopting commitments, often from parents, without having explored alternatives. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining status has a different pattern of the two dimensions. Trap: Confusing foreclosure with achievement because both show commitment.

qs.q: Which Eriksonian conflict follows identity?
qs.x: Correct: Young adulthood poses intimacy versus isolation immediately after the adolescent identity conflict. Why the others are wrong: The remaining conflicts belong to earlier or later stages. Trap: Skipping a stage in the sequence.

qs.q: What limits inference from this design?
o: That matches the stage of interest.
qs.x: Correct: A case series describes one group without a comparison, so differences cannot be attributed to any factor. Why the others are wrong: The status scheme, interview structure, and age range are appropriate choices. Trap: Criticizing a design feature that matches the research question.

qs.q: Which status is most common in this sample?
qs.x: Correct: Moratorium accounts for the largest share at 31%. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining status has a smaller share. Trap: Assuming achievement is most common because it is the mature status.

qs.q: Which added measure would test Erikson's sequencing claim?
o: Income is not a stage outcome.
qs.x: Correct: Erikson predicts that identity resolution supports later intimacy, so measuring intimacy across statuses tests the proposed order. Why the others are wrong: The remaining measures are covariates or procedural. Trap: Adding demographics instead of the next-stage outcome.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: Radioactive decay is first order: N = N₀(1/2)^(t/t½), where t½ is the half-life. In positron emission tomography (PET), ¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is taken up by metabolically active cells. ¹⁸F decays by positron emission with t½ = 110 min; each positron annihilates with an electron, producing two 511-keV photons in opposite directions.
A radiopharmacy prepared doses and measured activity over time (Table 1).

qs.q: What activity remains 440 minutes after preparation?
o: Activity decreases but does not reach zero.
qs.x: Correct: 440 min ÷ 110 min = 4 half-lives, so 400 × (1/2)⁴ = 25 MBq. Why the others are wrong: Each counts the wrong number of half-lives, or assumes complete decay. Trap: Mis-counting half-lives.

qs.q: Why must PET facilities be near a cyclotron?
o: The decay rate rises during transport
The rate falls as nuclei decay.
Cyclotrons are needed to detect the photons
The short half-life limits transport time
¹⁸F cannot be stored in any container
qs.x: Correct: With a 110-minute half-life, usable activity falls by half every two hours, so production must be close to use. Why the others are wrong: Detection uses the scanner; storage is possible; activity falls. Trap: Thinking decay rate increases with time.

qs.q: Why are two photons detected in opposite directions?
o: The detector creates a mirror image
Positrons travel in two directions at once
The nucleus emits two photons directly
qs.x: Correct: A positron and electron at rest have nearly zero net momentum, so the two 511-keV photons must leave in nearly opposite directions, which lets the scanner locate the event along a line. Why the others are wrong: The nucleus emits a positron; a positron has one path; the photons are physical. Trap: Attributing the photons to the nucleus.

qs.q: What particle is emitted in positron decay?
o: Neutron emission is a different process.
qs.x: Correct: Positron (β⁺) decay emits a positron and a neutrino as a proton converts to a neutron. Why the others are wrong: Alpha, γ and neutron emission are different decay modes. Trap: Confusing β⁺ with β⁻ or γ decay.

qs.q: Why does FDG accumulate in tumors?
o: Decay rate is independent of chemistry.
qs.x: Correct: FDG enters cells through glucose transporters and is phosphorylated but not metabolized further, so it accumulates where glucose uptake is high, as in many tumors. Why the others are wrong: It is not DNA-binding; tumors have vessels; decay rates are fixed. Trap: Thinking radioactive decay depends on the environment.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: In the photoelectric effect, light striking a metal ejects electrons only if the photon energy hf exceeds the work function φ. The maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons is KE = hf − φ, independent of intensity; intensity controls how many electrons are ejected. Here h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s.
Students shone monochromatic light on three metals and measured the stopping voltage, which equals the maximum electron kinetic energy in electron volts (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does zinc emit no electrons at either wavelength?
o: The light intensity was too low
Intensity does not set the threshold.
The threshold, not reflection, explains it.
Both photon energies are below 4.3 eV
qs.x: Correct: Photoemission requires hf > φ. At 4.13 eV and 2.48 eV, neither photon reaches zinc's 4.3-eV work function. Why the others are wrong: Metals have conduction electrons; intensity affects number, not threshold; the work function is the barrier. Trap: Expecting brighter light to overcome the threshold.

qs.q: What maximum kinetic energy would sodium electrons have at 250 nm (4.96 eV)?
qs.x: Correct: KE = hf − φ = 4.96 − 2.30 = 2.66 eV. Why the others are wrong: Each omits or misuses the work function. Trap: Adding the work function rather than subtracting it.

qs.q: Why does the photoelectric effect support a particle model of light?
o: That is diffraction, a wave property.
Intensity does not change the maximum energy.
Light travels at a fixed speed
qs.x: Correct: A wave model predicts that enough intensity would eventually eject electrons at any frequency. The observed sharp frequency threshold and intensity-independent kinetic energy require photons of energy hf. Why the others are wrong: Diffraction supports waves; intensity does not change maximum energy; the speed of light is common to both. Trap: Choosing a wave property.

qs.q: What does increasing light intensity change?
o: That is a property of the metal.
The threshold is fixed by φ.
The maximum kinetic energy of electrons
qs.x: Correct: More photons per second eject more electrons, but each photon still carries the same energy. Why the others are wrong: Kinetic energy depends on frequency; φ and the threshold are material properties. Trap: Mixing up the effects of frequency and intensity.

qs.q: Which metal would make the most sensitive detector for visible light?
o: Sodium, since it is a liquid metal
Sodium is solid at room temperature.
Cesium, with the lowest work function
Correct: visible photons can eject electrons.
All three work equally in visible light
Zinc, with the highest work function
Visible light cannot eject electrons from zinc.
qs.x: Correct: Visible photons carry roughly 1.7–3.1 eV, so only a metal with a work function below that range, such as cesium at 2.1 eV, responds across much of the visible spectrum. Why the others are wrong: Zinc's threshold is too high; sodium is solid; responses differ. Trap: Ignoring the photon energy range of visible light.

passages.title: Atoms, nuclear decay, electronic structure, and atomic chemical behavior · passage
text: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, the electron energy is Eₙ = −13.6 eV ÷ n². A photon is emitted when the electron drops from a higher level to a lower one, with energy equal to the difference. The Balmer series involves transitions ending at n = 2 and gives visible lines.
Students observed a hydrogen discharge lamp through a spectrometer and recorded wavelengths (Table 1). Photon energy in eV equals 1,240 divided by wavelength in nanometers.

qs.q: What photon energy corresponds to the n = 3 to n = 2 transition?
o: This is the n = 1 to n = 3 difference.
This is the ionization energy from n = 1.
qs.x: Correct: E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV and E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV, so the emitted photon carries 1.89 eV. Why the others are wrong: Each uses a single level or the wrong pair. Trap: Using a level energy instead of a difference.

qs.q: Why are Lyman series lines (ending at n = 1) in the ultraviolet?
o: They involve two photons at once
The electron gains energy in these transitions
qs.x: Correct: The n = 1 level lies far below the others, so transitions to it release 10 eV or more, corresponding to ultraviolet wavelengths. Why the others are wrong: Smaller differences are infrared; one photon is emitted; emission releases energy. Trap: Reversing the relation between energy and wavelength.

qs.q: What wavelength corresponds to a 10.2-eV photon?
o: This is the red Balmer line.
qs.x: Correct: λ = 1,240 ÷ 10.2 ≈ 122 nm, the n = 2 to n = 1 Lyman-α line. Why the others are wrong: Each misuses the relation. Trap: Forgetting that energy and wavelength are inversely related.

qs.q: Why does hydrogen produce discrete lines rather than a continuous spectrum?
o: The lamp filters out other colors
One electron can still give many lines.
Photons can carry only visible energies
qs.x: Correct: Because only certain energy levels are allowed, only specific energy differences, and therefore specific wavelengths, can be emitted. Why the others are wrong: Line structure comes from quantization, not electron count; no filter is used; photon energies are not limited to visible light. Trap: Attributing discreteness to having a single electron.

qs.q: Why does the Bohr model fail for multi-electron atoms?
o: Correct: energies depend on more than n.
It predicts no spectral lines at all
It predicts lines for hydrogen well.
qs.x: Correct: With more than one electron, mutual repulsion and shielding make energies depend on the orbital's shape as well as n, which the simple Bohr model does not include. Why the others are wrong: Quantization holds; electrons have mass; the model works for hydrogen. Trap: Rejecting the parts of the model that are correct.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: Boiling point reflects the strength of intermolecular forces. Hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O or F and a lone pair on an electronegative acceptor. Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules, and London dispersion forces grow with molar mass and surface contact. Branching lowers boiling point by reducing contact area.
Students measured boiling points of compounds with similar molar masses (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does 1-propanol boil higher than acetone despite similar molar mass?
o: It has a larger dipole moment only
The key difference is hydrogen bonding.
Acetone is a neutral polar molecule.
Correct: hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole-dipole forces.
It has more dispersion forces from branching
qs.x: Correct: 1-propanol has an O-H group that donates hydrogen bonds, which requires more energy to break than acetone's dipole-dipole attractions. Why the others are wrong: Dipole strength alone is not decisive; propanol is unbranched; acetone is molecular. Trap: Ranking forces by polarity without checking for an O-H or N-H donor.

qs.q: Why does 2-methyl-2-propanol boil lower than 1-propanol despite higher molar mass?
o: It cannot hydrogen bond at all
It is a gas at all temperatures
It has a lower molar mass
qs.x: Correct: The compact branched shape lowers the surface area available for dispersion forces and hinders hydrogen bonding, so the boiling point falls despite greater mass. Why the others are wrong: It does hydrogen bond; its mass is higher; it is a liquid at room temperature. Trap: Assuming boiling point always rises with molar mass.

qs.q: Which compound has only dispersion forces?
o: It has a polar carbonyl group.
qs.x: Correct: Butane's C-H and C-C bonds are essentially nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act. Why the others are wrong: The others have polar or hydrogen-bonding groups. Trap: Forgetting that dispersion forces exist in all molecules but dominate only in nonpolar ones.

qs.q: Why does dimethyl ether (46 g/mol) boil at −24 °C while ethanol (46 g/mol) boils at 78 °C?
o: Ethanol has a larger molar mass
Correct: the ether has no O-H.
It has a bent polar C-O-C unit.
The ether has more carbon atoms
qs.x: Correct: Both contain oxygen, but only ethanol has a hydrogen bonded to oxygen, so only ethanol can donate hydrogen bonds; the ether can only accept them. Why the others are wrong: The ether is polar; masses and carbon counts match. Trap: Assuming any oxygen-containing molecule hydrogen bonds strongly.

qs.q: Why is water's boiling point unusually high for its molar mass?
o: Each molecule makes several hydrogen bonds
Correct: two donors and two acceptor lone pairs.
Water forms covalent bonds between molecules
It has a molar mass of 18 g/mol.
qs.x: Correct: Each water molecule can donate two and accept two hydrogen bonds, producing an extensive network that requires much energy to disrupt. Why the others are wrong: Water is small and polar; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are not covalent. Trap: Explaining water's behavior by size rather than hydrogen bond count.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: Drug absorption depends on polarity. Nonpolar drugs cross lipid membranes readily but dissolve poorly in plasma; very polar or charged drugs do the opposite. The octanol-water partition coefficient, log P, measures lipophilicity. Ionizable drugs cross membranes mainly in their uncharged form, so pH matters.
Researchers measured properties of four candidate drugs (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does drug Y cross the monolayer less well than drug X despite being more lipophilic?
o: It is permanently charged in water
It is too polar to enter the membrane
It has a lower molar mass than X
Correct: very high log P hurts absorption.
qs.x: Correct: Permeability requires both membrane partitioning and aqueous solubility. With solubility of only 0.04 mg/mL, too little drug Y is dissolved to diffuse efficiently. Why the others are wrong: Y is lipophilic, not polar; no charge is stated; masses are not given. Trap: Assuming more lipophilic always means better absorbed.

qs.q: Why is drug W poorly permeable?
o: It has the highest log P
Its log P is the lowest.
It cannot dissolve in octanol or water
It is too insoluble in water
qs.x: Correct: A negative log P means the drug prefers water strongly, so it partitions poorly into the hydrophobic interior of the membrane. Why the others are wrong: Its water solubility is high and its log P is lowest. Trap: Mixing up the two ends of the solubility problem.

qs.q: Which drugs are in the favorable middle range of lipophilicity?
o: Correct: log P near 2 with good permeability.
qs.x: Correct: Drugs with log P roughly between 1 and 3 balance membrane partitioning against aqueous solubility; X and Z show the highest permeability. Why the others are wrong: W and Y are at the extremes. Trap: Choosing the highest log P as best.

qs.q: Aspirin is a weak acid with pKₐ 3.5. In the stomach at pH 2, what fraction is in the absorbable form?
o: Correct: pH below pKₐ favors the protonated form.
That occurs when pH equals pKₐ.
qs.x: Correct: For a weak acid, a pH below the pKₐ keeps most molecules protonated and neutral, so they cross the gastric mucosa more readily. Why the others are wrong: Ionization dominates above the pKₐ; half ionization occurs at pH = pKₐ. Trap: Reversing the Henderson-Hasselbalch reasoning for acids.

qs.q: Why is log P measured with octanol and water?
o: Octanol is more polar than water
Correct: it is a nonpolar phase.
qs.x: Correct: Octanol approximates the hydrophobic but slightly hydrogen-bonding environment of a lipid bilayer, so the partition ratio predicts membrane behavior. Why the others are wrong: Water is far more polar; octanol favors neutral species; the phases differ. Trap: Reversing which phase is polar.

passages.title: Nature of molecules and intermolecular interactions · passage
text: Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images with identical physical properties in achiral environments but different behavior in chiral environments such as enzyme active sites. A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both and shows no net optical rotation. Diastereomers differ at some but not all stereocenters and have different physical properties.
A pharmacology laboratory measured properties of two enantiomers of a drug and the racemate (Table 1).

qs.q: Why do the two enantiomers differ so much in receptor binding?
o: One has more atoms than the other
qs.x: Correct: A protein binding site is made of chiral amino acids, so it interacts differently with mirror-image ligands, giving binding constants that differ by more than 200-fold here. Why the others are wrong: Melting points, polarity and formulas are identical. Trap: Looking for a difference in bulk physical properties.

qs.q: Why does the racemate melt at a lower temperature than either enantiomer?
o: The racemate has a lower molar mass
The mixed crystal packs less efficiently
Correct: a different solid phase forms.
Mixtures always boil at lower temperatures too
qs.x: Correct: Enantiomers pack into separate, well-ordered crystals; the racemic solid has different packing and intermolecular contacts, which here lowers the melting point. Why the others are wrong: Both are stable; masses are equal; the boiling point did not change. Trap: Assuming a mixture lowers every transition temperature.

qs.q: Why does the racemate show zero optical rotation?
o: Light cannot pass through the mixture
The mixture is achiral at the molecular level
qs.x: Correct: A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers rotates plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, so the net rotation is zero even though every molecule is chiral. Why the others are wrong: Each enantiomer rotates light; light transmits; the molecules remain chiral. Trap: Concluding that zero rotation means no chiral molecules.

qs.q: Why are many drugs now sold as single enantiomers?
o: The inactive form may cause side effects
Correct: one enantiomer can be harmful.
qs.x: Correct: Because receptors and enzymes distinguish enantiomers, the unwanted form may be inactive or toxic, so purifying one enantiomer can improve safety and lower the dose. Why the others are wrong: Racemates are easy to make; single enantiomers often cost more; effects differ. Trap: Treating enantiomers as interchangeable.

qs.q: How could the enantiomers be separated?
qs.x: Correct: Converting enantiomers into diastereomeric salts with a chiral acid or base gives species with different solubilities and melting points, which can be separated and then reconverted. Why the others are wrong: Distillation and achiral recrystallization cannot distinguish them; measurement is not separation. Trap: Choosing a technique that relies on properties that are identical.
